metadata.author: Academy of Probate
metadata.shortDescription:
🏡 Ready to explore the lucrative world of wholesaling MLS properties in probate? You're in the right place! Welcome to the Academy of Probate's YouTube channel, where we'll guide you through every step of the process.

In this in-depth tutorial, we'll delve into the crucial aspects of probate property wholesaling:

1️⃣ Ethics and Fiduciary Duty to Client: Building a successful career in probate real estate starts with a strong foundation of ethics and a commitment to your fiduciary duty to clients. Learn the ins and outs of maintaining the highest ethical standards in the industry.

2️⃣ The Property Has Been Sitting for a Long Time: Discover the hidden gems among properties that have languished on the market. We'll show you how to identify these opportunities and turn them into profitable deals.

3️⃣ Property Condition and Appraisal Challenges: Many probate properties require substantial renovations and won't meet FHA, VA, or conventional appraisal standards. Find out how to assess property condition and navigate appraisal roadblocks with ease.

4️⃣ The Buyer Gives You a Bonus: One of the perks of being a probate real estate expert is the potential for bonuses from buyers. Learn effective negotiation strategies to maximize your earnings.

But wait, there's more! Subscribe to the Academy of Probate on YouTube and follow us on Instagram for a steady stream of valuable insights, tips, and updates on probate real estate. 📲

🎁 And here's the cherry on top: Get our FREE course on "How to Win the Probate Listing" to kickstart your journey. Plus, if you're ready to take your expertise to the next level, consider enrolling in our Certified Probate Real Estate Expert course www.academyofprobate.com/pages/CertifiedProbateRealEstateExpert.

Join us in mastering the art of probate real estate wholesale, and let's achieve success together. Subscribe, like, and hit the notification bell so you never miss a video. Have questions or suggestions? Drop them in the comments below, and we'll make sure to address them in future episodes. Let's make your probate real estate dreams a reality! 🌟 #ProbateRealEstate #Wholesaling #RealEstateSuccess

metadata.shortDescription:
Want more referrals from attorneys? Learn my 4-step plan to build powerful relationships with probate and trust attorneys, plus how it helped me land a $2M listing.

In today’s episode of Your Daily Real Estate Podcast, I break down the exact system I’ve used to consistently get high-quality leads from probate attorneys. It all began by chance and has now become my most valuable referral source.

Here’s what you’ll learn:
*   How to join professional referral networks the right way
*   What to say when reaching out to attorneys (without sounding like a desperate agent)
*   Why a custom trust and probate packet can set you apart
*   Tools you can use today to build impressive presentations
*   A twist most agents miss when trying to get in with attorneys
*   How to create shared value through joint education events
*   Ways to stay top of mind and build long-term trust

Spoiler: You don’t need to be pushy, you just need to show real value.

If you've ever wondered “How do I get consistent referrals from lawyers?” or “What do probate attorneys really want in a real estate partner?”, this one’s for you.

This episode is sponsored by abrillianttribe.com— where we help real estate professionals scale with smarter systems.

Listen to the full episode now: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/your-daily-real-estate-podcast-with-tristan-ahumada/id1719229930

Quick question for you: What’s been your biggest win, or mistake, when trying to connect with attorneys? Drop it in the comments.

Let’s grow smarter together. And hey, if you liked this one, catch the last episode in the playlist for more proven strategies that actually work.

0:00 4-Step Plan to Build Referral Partnerships with Probate & Trust Attorneys

metadata.shortDescription:
What is estate planning, and where should you start?

Kendra O’Toole, founding attorney at Legacy Legal Planning in Norwell, explains the essential documents, common misconceptions, and first steps Massachusetts families should know.

What’s one estate planning question you’ve always wanted to ask? 

Leave it in the comments, and subscribe for new videos every Wednesday!

Ready to take the next step with your estate plan?

Schedule a consultation with Legacy Legal Planning:
https://calendly.com/legacy-elizabeth/discovery-call

💜 FREE ESTATE PLANNING RESOURCES

Estate Planning 101 Checklist: https://legacylegalplanning.kit.com/estateplanningchecklist
Babysitter Checklist: https://legacylegalplanning.kit.com/bf1a2778d1
Nursing Home Community Checklist: https://legacylegalplanning.kit.com/4180514414
Legacy Legal Library: https://legacylegalplanning.com/legacy-legal-library/


LEARN MORE ABOUT LEGACY LEGAL PLANNING
https://legacylegalplanning.com/

CONNECT WITH US
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/legacylegalplanning
TikTok: https://www.tiktok.com/@legacylegalplanning
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/legacylegalplanning
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/legacylegalplanning/

ABOUT LEGACY LEGAL PLANNING

Legacy Legal Planning is a Massachusetts estate planning and elder law firm helping individuals and families understand their options and create plans designed for their lives, their families, and their legacies.

The information provided in this video is for general educational and informational purposes only and should not be considered legal advice. Viewing this video does not create an attorney-client relationship. Every situation is different, and laws may change. Please consult with a qualified attorney regarding your individual circumstances.

Starting an estate sale business can be a rewarding venture,
but it requires careful planning and execution.
Here are ten tips to help you launch and run a successful estate sale business:
1. Research and Education: - Before diving in,
thoroughly research the estate sale industry. Understand the legal and ethical aspects,
pricing strategies, and best practices. Attend workshops or online courses to gain knowledge
about antiques, collectibles, and estate sale management.
2. Legal Considerations: - Familiarize yourself with
local regulations and obtain any necessary licenses or permits. Ensure that you comply
with tax laws and any other legal requirements for conducting estate sales in your area.
3. Build a Network: - Establish relationships
with local estate planning professionals, real estate agents, and attorneys. Networking can help
you gain referrals and build a client base. Attend industry events and join relevant online forums.
4. Develop Organizational Skills: - Estate sales involve managing a large
volume of items. Develop efficient systems for cataloging, organizing, and displaying
items. Invest in inventory management software to help streamline the process.
5. Pricing Expertise: - Develop a pricing strategy
based on thorough research of market values for various items. Consider hiring an appraiser for
valuable or unique items. Transparent and fair pricing will build trust with your clients.
6. Marketing and Advertising: - Create a professional website and
use social media platforms to showcase your services. Develop a strong online presence
by posting photos of past sales and positive client testimonials. Utilize local newspapers,
community bulletin boards, and online classifieds to reach a broader audience.
7. Customer Service: - Provide excellent
customer service to both clients and buyers. Clear communication,
responsiveness, and professionalism will enhance your reputation and encourage repeat business.
8. Effective Merchandising: - Display items in an organized
and aesthetically pleasing manner. Create a welcoming atmosphere that encourages buyers
to explore and make purchases. Consider arranging items by category or theme.
9. Security Measures: - Implement security measures
to protect both the estate and the items for sale. This may include hiring security personnel,
using surveillance cameras, or having a controlled entry system for the sale.
10. Flexible Payment Options: - Offer multiple payment options
such as cash, credit cards, and online payments to accommodate a wider range of
buyers. Clearly communicate your payment policies to both clients and buyers.
Remember that the estate sale business requires adaptability and a commitment to providing
value to your clients and customers. Building a strong reputation takes time, so be patient and
stay dedicated to delivering quality services. That concludes the video. Now it’s time you get

It is completely free, no strings attached. Thanks for watching, If you found this video
useful, please like and subscribe so you don't miss any future content.

metadata.title: Estate Sale Planning Basics: How to Clear Out a Home Without Feeling Overwhelmed
metadata.author: At Home with Jody
metadata.shortDescription:
🏡 Estate Sale Planning: How to Clear Out a Home Without Feeling Overwhelmed

Are you staring at a home full of furniture, collections, and decades of memories and thinking… “Where do I even start?” 😩

You’re not alone.

🏡Estate sale planning can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re downsizing, settling an estate, or preparing a home for sale after a major life transition. In this video, I break down estate sale planning step by step so you can move forward with clarity and confidence.
________________________________________________________________________

📦 In This Video, You’ll Learn:

✔ What estate sale planning actually involves
✔ When hiring an estate sale company makes sense
✔ Common estate sale planning mistakes to avoid 🚫
✔ How estate sale companies price, stage, and sell contents
✔ Alternatives to estate sales, including auctions and online sales
✔ How estate sale planning fits into selling a home 🏠

________________________________________________________________________

CHAPTERS 
00:00 - Introduction 
01:13 – What is an Estate Sale?
02:19 - Preparing a Home for an Estate Sale
05:33 – Your Estate Sale Options
08:24 – Hiring an Estate Sale Company
09:28- Common Estate Sale Mistakes to Avoid
11:17 – What Comes After the Estate Sale?

________________________________________________________________________

🧠 Who This Video Is For:

👵 Empty nesters & downsizers
👨‍👩‍👧 Families settling an estate
📦 Anyone overwhelmed by “too much stuff”
🏡 Homeowners preparing a house for sale with contents inside

If you’re clearing out a home after a parent passes away, preparing for a move, or just trying to simplify life, estate sale planning can save you time, stress, and costly mistakes.

________________________________________________________________________
ABOUT JODY & CONTACT INFORMATION:

JODY WHITEHURST, Broker 
☎️ PHONE/TEXT: (919) 830-4622
📧 EMAIL: whitehurstjody@gmail.com 
💻 WEBSITE: www.jodywhitehurstrealestate.com

ℹ️ About Me
Hi, I'm Jody.  I am a Keller Williams Luxury Designated Realtor in Apex, NC and the Greater Raleigh area of North Carolina. I specialize in helping Empty Nesters and Downsizers make confident, cost-effective decisions when preparing their homes for sale and navigate the emotional and task-related preparation of their home sale. ❤️🏡

📍 Serving Raleigh, Apex, Cary, Holly Springs, Fuquay, Pittsboro, Durham, Chapel Hill, Garner, and many other towns around the Greater Triangle Area

📍 A Quick Note on Location:

I help homeowners navigate estate sale planning as part of downsizing and preparing homes for sale. While I’m based in the Triangle area of North Carolina —including Raleigh, Cary, and Apex—the guidance in this video applies no matter where you live.

💬 Let’s Keep the Conversation Going:

If you’re feeling stuck, overwhelmed, or unsure what to do next—you don’t have to figure it out alone. Please reach out if there is anything that I can help you with during this transition.

JODY WHITEHURST, Broker (Luxury Designated)
☎️ PHONE/TEXT: (919) 830-4622
📧 EMAIL: whitehurstjody@gmail.com 
💻 WEBSITE: www.jodywhitehurstrealestate.com

👇 Drop your questions in the comments
👍 Like this video if it was helpful
🔔 Subscribe for more downsizing, home prep, and real-life real estate guidance

Inherited a home and don't know where to start? Here is the complete guide on selling inherited property smoothly while avoiding major legal and tax mistakes.

Serving as an executor comes with a unique weight. We also explain how the step-up in basis eliminates capital gains tax when selling inherited property.

06:10 How Alix Helps Executors Save Time & Reduce Stress

metadata.title: What Happens If You Start an Estate Sale Company
metadata.author: Gyd Path
metadata.shortDescription:
An estate sale company looks simple from the outside, but behind every folding table, cardboard sign, price tag, jewelry case, crowded driveway and emptied house exists a system built across trust, pricing judgment, family conflict, buyer psychology, traffic control, inventory security, cleanout deadlines and the emotional pressure of selling someone’s life room by room.

What Happens If You Start an Estate Sale Company follows the progression from weekend sale helper into lead staging, solo liquidation, full-service estate sales, high-end neighborhood work, auction warehousing, regional luxury liquidation and eventually an estate liquidation empire built around specialists, warehouses, trucks, appraisers, security and multi-city sale control.

This episode is built for viewers who want to understand why estate sales are not just weekend garage sales, how one wrong price can hand profit to a dealer, why families can become the hardest part of the job, and how the business changes when dusty household rooms turn into jewelry control, private previews, auction systems and trustee-level liquidation.

The first level begins with the most fragile part of the business: trust inside someone else’s home. Helpers carry furniture, tag mugs, watch bedrooms, handle bargain hunters and stand near the cash box while valuables can disappear and blame moves faster than proof. Before the company has systems, it survives on attention, honesty and the ability to stay calm when a family looks for someone to blame.

The staging and solo stages turn messy houses into controlled sales floors. Clothing racks, maker marks, clean labels, sold comps, dealer behavior, pickup tickets, donation piles, family keepsakes and disputed furniture all decide whether the sale creates value or chaos. The operator learns that pricing is not decoration; pricing is power, and every room needs rules before strangers enter it.

The full-service stage adds crowd control and liability. Radios, jewelry zones, checkout lanes, pickup cones, donation trucks, realtor deadlines, neighbor complaints, inspector warnings, parking maps and permit binders show that an estate sale can become a traffic event as much as a retail event. The company is no longer just selling objects; it is controlling people, cars, access, money and risk around a private property.

The high-end stage raises the stakes because privacy becomes part of the product. Mansion gates, numbered tickets, designer racks, diamond trays, art appraisers, firearms rooms, private previews, vehicle titles and security cameras turn the sale into a controlled market for wealthy heirs and serious buyers. At this level, one dishonest crew member or one hidden phone photo can damage more than the day’s revenue.

The auction warehouse stage changes the model again. Estate goods move through loading docks, scanner checks, photo stations, lot descriptions, high-value trays, pickup lanes, packing tables, shipping scales and online bidder disputes. The sale no longer ends when buyers leave the driveway; damage claims, chargebacks, condition reports and one-star reviews can reach back into the warehouse and attack the margin after the auction closes.

This is the reality most people misunderstand. Behind every serious estate sale company exists appraisal judgment, item security, family access rules, buyer management, traffic planning, contract language, commission control, cleanout coordination, warehouse flow, auction photography, shipping standards, specialist scheduling, privacy protection, proof binders and manager authority that buyers never see while browsing a staged living room.

This episode is designed for viewers researching the business beneath estate sales rather than the public image of dusty tables and bargain hunters. It shows how homes become marketplaces, how grief and money collide inside ordinary rooms, how pricing mistakes create silent losses, how online auctions add new risk, and how a local liquidator can grow into a trusted company managing entire estates across multiple cities.

Subscribe to Gyd Path for business systems, hidden industry mechanics, ownership breakdowns, and level-by-level documentaries explaining how modern industries operate behind the scenes.

You check the utility watch exactly on time at the door. At the entry rope, an early buyer leans over and demands garage access. You run checkout through the portable card reader beside stacked forms. At the label printer, you make clean tags for watches and tools. You read $4,000 per month on the payroll stub in your apartment. Inside the locking jewelry case, you secure bracelets and watches. You face a collector who pushes the vinyl stack forward and demands a bundle discount. Before pickup, you pin the pickup ticket to a sold dresser. You tag the walnut chair below market after skimming sold comps. At the open front doorway, you watch movers carry the walnut chair away. You open the dealer listing photo and see five times your price. In the kitchen, you slam the laptop shut and breathe hard. You listen as your boss taps the coffee mug and defends fast sales over perfect prices. Under kitchen light, you trace the furniture brand stamp from memory. You reset the dining table before the second wave enters. Outside your apartment, you park beside van shelves in the apartment lot. You inspect brass through the jeweler's loop and separate collectible pieces. Across the table, a shopper shoves a lamp forward and accuses you of changing tags. You photograph the dealer resale page with your phone outside. After closing, you buy a black pocket notebook from a drugstore. You fill notebook columns with brands, neighborhoods, chair shapes, and buyer names. Before the walk-through, you slip the notebook into your work bag. Level three, solo liquidator. You roll the storage unit door above tables, racks, bins, and signs. At the curb, you plant the crooked logo yard sign. You strap folding tables inside the enclosed trailer without wasting space. Before sunrise, you drive the used pickup through older streets. You unlock the house alone while strangers gather beneath the front lawn sign. Near the sewing machine, a grieving heir guards the cabinet and asks for mercy. You mark donation piles with yellow stickers room by room. Beside the camera tripod, you photograph lamps, tools, rugs, and China. You write your company name on the first invoice. In the dining room, you direct laborers around the China cabinet. You place the rare tool tray near checkout under your watch. At the table, a buyer waves the printed preview page and demands the expired price. You carry the deposit slip at the bank and see $7,000 for the month. At the kitchen counter, you count bills while buyers carry rugs outside. You hang logo staff shirts from the closet rod. After spotting originals, you price the ornament box higher. You tape a red sold sign beside the dresser for pickup. Across the dining room, one sibling points at the set and says, "Never sell." You pause the checkout line during the driveway family argument. In the driveway, siblings shout until one threatens cancellation. You walk toward both sides with the house keys held high. At the removal sheet, you require both heirs' signatures first. You leave the photo album untouched beside receipts. At the bedroom door, you lock the knob and redirect buyers to garage tables. You load donation boxes with books and appliances after closing. Inside storage, you add the second rack row from sale profits. You hear a landlord tap the clipboard and demand Monday clearance. At your desk, you work the call list through a hauler, a charity truck, and a buyer. You sweep the empty duplex floor while your trailer waits outside. Under the porch light, you spread dirty hands blackened with dust, ink, and insulation. You face a condo hallway crowd surging toward your smallest advertised sale. Through the cramped kitchen, you turn one-way checkout arrows toward the exit. You listen as a neighbor points at the blocked mailbox and complains about buyers. After a slow Friday, you hammer the corner sign stake. You study the printed schedule with three estates across two weekends. On the trailer ramp, you wipe sweat with a receipt. You mark family items with a blue tape strip before buyers touch them. On the pickup truck, you sign the broom-clean checklist. You recount the cash box total after an heir taps the slip and demands proof. Before accepting more work, you add family access rules to the revised contract. >> Level four, full-service estate sale company. You sit across the probate folder while heirs debate commission terms. At the branded box truck, you direct the crew loading dollies and racks. You clip the insurance certificate to the contract page. Beside the calculator, the accountant taps totals and says commissions cleared $15,000 for the month. You assign staff radios to jewelry, checkout, pickup, and crowd control. At the warehouse bay, you list the door past packed shelves. You check the jewelry safe bolted beneath the security camera. Around the house, buyers form a block-long line for the rooms turned department store. You price the garage tool table from comps and contractor demand. During the rush, you station crew at the glass jewelry case. You watch a realtor tap the lock box and pressure you for Monday listing photos. Before opening, you drape matching shirts over folding chairs. You coordinate the dump trailer beside donation trucks in the side yard. Along the driveway, you set pickup lane cones for furniture flow. You face a neighbor thrusting photo printouts of cars across her driveway. For faster movement, you move the checkout table closer to the front door. You confront the inspector's badge at the curb over traffic complaints. In the street, you redirect cars with one raised arm. You listen as the inspector marks the citation pad and warns about emergency access. Through the radio earpiece, you cap entry and order the crew to move signs. You meter buyers with porch entry counters while the line bends around corners. Along the curb, you place orange cones as a traffic plan. You tape paid tags along the foyer runner. At the entry, a shopper grips the numbered card and yells about crowd limits. You separate jewelry receipt book pages from general household checkout. From the security camera feed, you review racks, shelves, supplies, and coverage. You guide the warehouse broom through a broom clean handoff. Beside contracts, you set the permit binder within reach. You answer a part-time worker who waves the time card and questions driveway rules. Beside the warning notice, you snap the binder shut. You sketch the parking map for the next sale. At the equipment crate, you pack radios, ropes, cones, and cases. You place the liability waiver atop the revised family packet. Outside, the driver eases the branded truck away as porch lights warm the packed house. You lock the warehouse company sign behind the rented bay door. After the citation, you add permits, parking plans, and neighbor notices to every proposal packet. Level five, high-end neighborhood specialist. You open the mansion gate on ropes, jewelry security, tickets, and a sold sports car. Outside the lake house, you park the late model pickup beside the branded truck. You plant professional signposts along the private road instead of arrows. At the velvet tray, a jewelry specialist studies diamonds under your supervision. You check the numbered ticket stack before dealers pass the rope. Across the privacy agreement, a wealthy heir demands both discretion and turnout. You inspect the handbag display case with individual security tags. In the dining room, you bring the art appraiser's light to signatures. You require movers to wrap the marble table in a moving blanket. At the rope, a dealer waves the preview invitation and complains about unfair access. You read $35,000 for the month on the daily total receipt at checkout. Besides designer racks, you check the climate control gauge. You watch a coin expert sort bullion on the felt mat. Before public opening, you escort top buyers with private preview badges. You take the vehicle title from a collector who grips it and refuses to leave. Before noon, you tag the sports car windshield with the sold tag. You secure firearms in the lockbox inside the controlled room. At the radio charging dock, you monitor zones as staff report coverage. You notice the senior crew badge clipped to his lanyard on the schedule. During preview, you catch a hidden phone screen photographing valuable items. You take the dealer contact card when the crew lead offers it and admits the tip. At once, you yank the staff badge and walk the lead to the gate. You aim the security camera dome above jewelry at the doorway. Before buyers enter, you match photos to each inventory number tag. You check watches from the locked room individually at the log. Across the marble foyer, a designer argues over the sofa price. You guide lake house buyers through art, rugs, clothing, and crystal. Inside warehouse storage, you inspect cages for rugs, art, jewelry, and watches. You install the control checklist before the next mansion sale. Level six, auction warehouse operator. You guide two box trucks beside the cargo van at the loading dock. Under bright lights, crews move estate goods through the warehouse assembly line. You require inventory scanner checks before furniture reaches auction shelves. From the floor, you study pallet racks above chairs, rugs, trunks, and art. You route crews around the forklift through marked aisles. At the auction monitor wall, you watch the system display $80,000 for the month. You have the photographer light the watch photo booth for every scratch. Near the pickup board, the warehouse manager points at the schedule and objects. You watch packers wrap items at the packing table. In the back room, you inspect jewelry safes lined like bank equipment. You review the high value lot tray before descriptions go live. At the art photo station, you assign categories to separate stations. You face a seller waving a complaint email printout over plain looking antiques. On the platform, the auction software counts down as bidders fight over watches, art, and signs. You track branded uniform patches moving through booths, shelves, benches, and dock doors. From the dispatch wall map, you send crews to cleanouts. You watch shipping staff build foam corner inserts around fragile porcelain figurines. At the dock desk, a driver slaps the timesheet down and refuses a late pickup. You manage the warehouse pickup lane while trucks unload behind buyers. At the shelf, you read lot numbers on staff tablets. You place pickup divider signs before checkout chaos starts. On the table, you open photos of the shattered collectible box. You receive a chargeback notice from the buyer demanding a refund and reviews. Beside the packing manual, you spread broken porcelain photos. You listen as the shipping lead points to the old packing checklist. With foam, void fill, and labels, you test the double box sample. You read the one-star review screen beside lunch. At the shipping scale, you reweigh packages before staff relabel shelves. You keep the warehouse moving while camera bulbs flash, drivers turn forklifts, and bids climb. Through the warehouse office window, you study stations, shelves, benches, and traffic. You receive a damage claim form from an online bidder challenging the description. After the claim, you add condition report templates to every high-value lot. You unload blanket-wrapped furniture from returning trucks at night. Before packages leave, you check the shipping bay camera. You call the angry buyer personally through the phone headset. Across the desk, the accountant highlights the refund spreadsheet and warns about margin. You mark red fragile labels before cataloging begins. Before dawn, you restock shelves using auction shelf labels. You review a drone camera feed showing trucks, docks, lights, and buyer cars. Beside damaged item photos, you hang the training poster. You stage the three-vehicle lineup under the warehouse sign before dispatch. Before chasing more volume, you build the systems binder. Level seven, regional luxury liquidator. You step from the airport lounge doorway toward the rental SUV. Beyond garage and wine cellar doors. Sunrise washes the hilltop mansion. You listen as a trustee taps the briefcase and warns that competitors want the celebrity contract. Inside the SUV, you hang the tailored jacket beside ranch boots. You walk the specialist floor plan through art, jewelry, vehicles, and designer rooms. On the video call phone, you brief warehouse chiefs before openings. You watch crews raise three sale banners in different cities at the same hour. At the calendar wall, a luxury realtor marks the launch date and demands alignment. You add a hotel key card to the stack from last week. Beside you, the finance partner shows the tablet and says revenue is $180,000 for the month. You ride between ranch, condo, and collector home while the dashboard tracks the route. During the walkthrough, you spot the bronze sculpture misfiled as decor. You answer a family office representative challenging the security transport plan. Across Interstate exits, branded trucks head toward separate luxury estates. You read department door labels across jewelry, art, furniture, and shipping. At the boardroom table, you meet attorneys above the downtown district. You sequence the regional calendar wall with travel, hotels, trucks, and security. From another state, a crew chief calls about absent movers. You make the expensive rescue call outside the airport curb. Along the wine cellar rack, you mark rare bottles. You inventory a covered classic, a golf cart, motorcycles, and tools inside the six-car garage. From the drone feed, you review the mansion, trucks, buyer tents, and security gates. You balance the trustee's demand for speed against the appraiser gripping the clipboard. At the closet rack, you divide items into sale, private, and authentication piles. You carry garment bags and estate binders at check-in. Among airport gate seats, burnout catches you during a missed family event. You stare at the missed call screen before the jet bridge. On voicemail, the operations manager says airport approvals cannot continue. You flatten the wrinkled boarding pass beside the access fob. From above, you watch the regional warehouse floor buzzing across departments. You pin the jewelry lead badge with approval authority. In the conference room, you arrange nameplates for regional leads. You face a senior specialist pointing at the reporting chart and demanding access. Across the city map, illuminated markers show open estates in multiple cities. You cut duplicate keyrings for warehouses, safes, and sale houses. Beside the driveway, you record instructions on the field checklist card. You dispatch trucks from hotel parking lots toward estates at dawn. After the briefing, you hand the radio to a regional lead and step back. You hear an attorney tap the pen and question whether the company can function without you. Before boarding the next flight, you sign the authority sheet. Level eight, estate liquidation empire owner. You step from the executive SUV in tailored clothes for a walk-through. Before sunrise, crews load the fleet lined across the warehouse yard. You direct managers across docks, aisles, and bays from the radio board. Beneath city, client, and sale date signs, you walk furniture rows. You review the estate packet with attorneys while teams inventory assets. Across the table, a trustee taps the property list and asks about speed without chaos. You watch technicians raise live bid screens as buyers move through staged warehouse aisles. Beside you, a family office executive shows the tablet. $500,000 per month across services. You verify the biometric lock beneath white appraisal lights. Under the mansion banner, you send carts through the gated estate. You match collector seating cards to art lots before the auction opens. On the conference table, a rival proposal folder undercuts your commission. You open the buyer directory carried by the account manager. Across three markets, managers open mansion sales while dashboards glow. You cross the loading dock walkway while managers brief you. At your side, a family attorney adjusts his glasses and questions the cheaper national competitor. You bring the specialist lineup forward for jewelry, vehicles, books, art, firearms, and logistics. After the walk-through, you host dinner at the private table by lake windows. You check each security access badge on department leads. From dispatch, you split truck routes between condos and estates. You review drone footage showing warehouses, trucks, lines, and mansion gates. On your phone, you read the cancellation email promising faster cleanout from the rival. You call leads for proof at the boardroom doorway. Across the room, a national sales rep drops a business card and smirks about local speed. You lead the tour route past placards for warehouse, security, auction, shipping, and appraisal. On the live tour, staff show trucks, appraisers, cameras, and bidders working. You light the classic car with portable inspection lamps. Beside pickup, you monitor sealed shipping cartons leaving with customer service. You answer the rival's challenge to reach by pointing at the national bid map. From the panoramic aisle, you show racks, safes, rows, and shipping bays. You split the estate chart into five streams before the family. Beside the silver signing pen, you place the contract. You slide the proof binder to the family matriarch in silence. Across from you, the matriarch touches her pearls and asks about dignity, privacy, and control. You assign the specialist schedule card with manager, security, and specialists. From regional offices, staff confirm lodging, routes, auction slots, and access. You leave the closed rival folder at the table's far end. Inside the estate room, you sign while logo trucks wait beyond the gates. You watch crews unlock mansions in three cities as buyers line behind ropes. Through warehouse rows, you direct camera-lit treasures under staff control. You monitor auctions, trucks, and buyer counts at the screen wall. At dawn, your drivers roll the fleet as auctions, mansions, buyer lines, and the empire move together.

metadata.shortDescription:
Estate sale liquidation is a big industry...there are never enough companies that provide this service to those who need it. Estate sale liquidation was rated in the Top 3 Home-Based Businesses in the United States. Entrance into the industry is simple, the initial investment is low and the demandd is very high. The only question is - how do you get started? My Jennarocity Estate Sales is a liquidation company started by Jenna Pecor in 2015. She's been providing estate liquidation services in her hometown of Grand Prairie and now, she's put together a course that teaches you how to start a company in your local community. You'll get videos, lessons and a first-hand look of what it really looks like to hold an estate liquidation sale. 

Click here to learn how to become an estate liquidation provider: https://www.jennapecor.com/train-to-become-an-estate-sale-provider

See how EstateSail brings your entire estate sale together—from inventory and pricing to checkout and selling online.

In this full walkthrough, founder Ryan Root takes you through the EstateSail mobile app, web app, and marketplace, showing how they work together to help estate liquidators run more sales in less time.

Explore how to:
• Create and manage estate sales
• Build inventory with AI-powered descriptions and price suggestions
• Print barcode labels and streamline in-person checkout
• Manage your sales across the mobile and web apps
• Bring your inventory online through the EstateSail marketplace
• Track sales and simplify client reporting

Built by a liquidator for liquidators, EstateSail connects the work you do before, during, and after every sale in one platform.

Learn more: https://learn.estatesail.us
Email: ryan@estatesail.us

Book a one-on-one demo: https://calendar.app.google/Fn4yRYqnhWYATNaf8

metadata.title: Can Medicaid Take Your Parents’ House After They Die?
metadata.author: MarcCormier
metadata.shortDescription:
Can Medicaid take your parent's house?
Usually not while your parent is alive. After they die, though, the state can file a claim against the house to recover what Medicaid paid for long-term care, and a paid-off home is often the biggest thing in the estate. In this video I explain how estate recovery works in Maryland, Virginia and DC, with the legal sources on screen.

📋 Free one-page checklist: Help34.com

**Key numbers**
• In 2026, you can't qualify for long-term care Medicaid if your home equity is over $752,000 in Maryland and Virginia, or $1.13 million in DC. This doesn't apply when a spouse, a minor, or a disabled child lives in the home.
• Starting January 1, 2028, federal law caps that limit at $1 million, with no increases for inflation. DC's limit drops. Maryland and Virginia are already under the cap.
• The claim is paid out of the sale. It changes what the family walks away with, so know the amount before you price the house.

**Chapters**
0:00 Linda's letter
0:22 Why I'm making this
0:50 The myth
1:22 Estate recovery
1:52 Why paid-off homes
2:18 Your state
2:36 Maryland
2:51 Virginia
3:02 DC
3:16 What happens at the sale
3:34 If you get the letter
4:25 Protect the house the right way
5:00 The 2028 change
5:43 How Linda's story ended
6:15 Recap

**Related questions**

**What should I do if we get a Medicaid estate recovery letter?**
Don't ignore it, and don't pay it before you check it. Ask for an itemized statement of what Medicaid actually paid, see whether any protections apply, and get the waiver deadline in writing.

**Who is protected from estate recovery?**
Recovery is delayed or blocked while there's a surviving spouse, a child under 21, or a blind or disabled child. Maryland law also requires the claim to be waived when it would cause substantial hardship to surviving dependents.

**Can I just put the house in my kids' names?**
Not on your own. A transfer can cause a Medicaid penalty, and the kids can lose the step-up in tax basis they'd get by inheriting. There are legal exceptions: a transfer to a spouse, to a child under 21, to a blind or disabled child, to a sibling who co-owns the home and lived there a year, or to a caregiver child who lived there two years. Every one of them needs an elder law attorney.

**Does it matter which state you live in?**
Yes. Maryland ties the claim to the probate estate and can place a lien during life. Virginia uses a broader definition of the estate that can reach past probate. DC can collect on a home lien only after the home is sold and no spouse, minor child or disabled child lives there.

**About Marc**
Marc Cormier is a licensed real estate professional with Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices PenFed Realty, based in Montgomery County, Maryland. He has 27+ years of experience and has closed 800+ transactions, with a focus on probate, distressed properties, bankruptcy trustee sales, and downsizing for families across Maryland, DC, and Northern Virginia. He is the author of an Amazon best-selling book on probate real estate and holds the SRES (Seniors Real Estate Specialist) designation.

📞 Selling an inherited house with a Medicaid claim? Call Marc Cormier, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices PenFed Realty:
Office (MD): 301-660-6272 ext. 711
Office (VA): 703-445-3550 ext. 711
🌐 Help34.com

**Sources shown in the video**
• Federal: 42 U.S.C. §1396p(a), (b), (c); 26 U.S.C. §§1014, 1015
• Maryland: COMAR 10.09.24.15A(4), 15A-2(2); Md. Health-Gen. §15-121(b)
• Virginia: 12VAC30-20-141
• DC: DC Department of Health Care Finance, Estate Recovery fact sheet
• Home-equity limits: CMS 2026 SSI and spousal impoverishment standards; Pub. L. 119-21 §71108 (Virginia and DC figures pending state confirmation)
• Care costs: CareScout (Genworth) 2025 Cost of Care Survey

**Disclaimer:** Marc Cormier is a licensed real estate agent with Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices PenFed Realty, not an attorney. This video is general education, not legal, tax or financial advice. Rules change and every family's situation is different, so talk to an elder law attorney licensed in your state before you act. "Linda" is a hypothetical example, not a real client.

metadata.title: Medicaid Estate Recovery: 7 Ways to Protect Your Family Home Before 2027
metadata.author: Carol Benning
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you worried that Medicaid might claim your family home? Federal law permits estate recovery for those 55 and older, but specific statutory exemptions exist to help you protect your residence.

⏱️ CHAPTERS
0:00 A paid-off home is often the primary target for Medicaid est
2:26 #1 Understanding Medicaid Estate Recovery
5:52 #2 Exemptions for Your Family
9:19 #3 The Caregiver Exemption
12:13 #4 Asking for a Hardship Waiver
15:49 #5 Using Partnership Policies
17:38 #6 Navigating Equity Caps
20:04 #7 Why Planning Early Matters
22:04 Your checklist
25:45 Final word

✅ WHAT WE COVER
• Medicaid estate recovery rules for seniors
• Spousal and child exemptions under 42 USC
• Caregiver child rule requirements
• How to apply for hardship waivers
• Long-term care partnership program benefits
• Understanding the 60-month look-back period
• Home equity limits for Medicaid eligibility
• Difference between Medicare and Medicaid coverage
• Legal strategies to keep your home in the family
• Why wills often fail to protect assets
• Managing estate recovery notices and timelines
• The role of elder law attorneys in planning
• How to document care provided at home

📚 OFFICIAL SOURCES
• Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (medicaid.gov)
• Social Security Administration (ssa.gov)
• 42 U.S. Code Section 1396p (Estate Recovery Laws)
• Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 (CMS.gov)
• Federal Trade Commission (consumer.ftc.gov)

The people in our examples are composites. Figures come from official U.S. government sources listed above. This video is for general information only and is not financial, legal or medical advice. Check your own situation with the agency concerned.

metadata.title: Will My Home Even Qualify for a Reverse Mortgage? Condo, Trust, Manufactured Home
metadata.author: The Retirement Loan Guy
metadata.shortDescription:
You're 62 or older and you've wondered about a reverse mortgage, but you live in a condo, or your house is in a family trust, or the roof is tired. So you assumed the answer was no and never made the call. This video explains what actually decides whether a home qualifies for a reverse mortgage (HECM), so you can find out before you spend a dime.

You will learn:

*Why not every home qualifies, and why qualifying is not the same as being approved
*The four checkpoints: you, the home type, how it's owned, and its condition
*Which home types generally work, and which generally don't: single-family homes, 2-4 unit properties, FHA-approved condos, manufactured homes, co-ops
*Why many living trusts are fine, and what a lender and title company will want to review
*What happens when the home needs repairs, and why the appraisal matters
*Three made-up example homes with three different answers (illustrative only)
*The catches: costs up front, a condo that needs its whole building approved, a balance that grows over time, and taxes, insurance and upkeep that stay yours

A reverse mortgage isn't right for everyone, and if your home or your situation isn't a fit, I'll tell you so. My job is honest, plain-English guidance so you can decide with confidence.

Chapters
0:00 Will your home even qualify?
0:40 Who this is for: you assumed the answer was no
1:25 My favorite loan, hard parts first
2:48 The four checkpoints
3:44 Checkpoint 2: the home type
4:28 How it's owned, and its condition
5:48 Three example homes
6:52 The catches, told straight
8:13 Where this lands

📅 Not sure if your home qualifies? Tell me about it and I'll give you a straight answer. Book a free, no-obligation call: https://book-with-david.netlify.app/

David Todd · Mortgage Loan Officer · NMLS #2645936 · Honest reverse mortgage guidance for homeowners 62 and older in North Carolina.

MCM Capital Solutions · Company NMLS #213236 · NC L-199179 · David Todd NMLS #2645936 / NC I-225310

#ReverseMortgage #HECM #HomeEquity

— This video is for educational purposes and is not a commitment to lend. A reverse mortgage (HECM) is a home-secured loan. Eligibility depends on HUD and FHA guidelines, which change, and on the property, its title and ownership, its condition, and the borrower. The examples shown are made-up and illustrative only; they are not a promise that any home qualifies. The loan balance grows over time and upfront costs apply. You remain responsible for property taxes, homeowners insurance, and maintaining the home, and the home must be your primary residence. HUD-approved independent counseling is required before a HECM application can proceed. Consultation is free with no obligation. Equal Housing Opportunity.

metadata.title: Medicaid Estate Recovery: A Primer
metadata.author: Community Legal Services of Philadelphia
metadata.shortDescription:
Community Legal Services of Philadelphia's introduction to PA's Medicaid Estate Recovery Program. Funded by Philadelphia Corporation for the Aging.

For more information about Pennsylvania's Medicaid Estate Recovery Program, please visit http://clsphila.org/get-help/medical-assistance-estate-recovery-program.

More information about Community Legal Services can be found on our website at www.clsphila.org. 

To get legal help, visit www.clsphila.org/get-help

Disclaimer:
This video provides information to help Pennsylvania residents resolve their legal problems. The information in this video is not legal advice. Legal information is not the same as legal advice, which is the application of law to an individual's specific circumstances. The information in this video is not a substitute for and does not replace the advice or representation of a licensed attorney. Although CLS goes to great lengths to make sure the information in this video is accurate and up to date, we make no claim as to the accuracy of this information and are not responsible for any consequences that may result from the use of this video. We recommend that you consult with a licensed attorney if you want assurance that the information in this video and your interpretation of it are appropriate for your particular situation. You should not and are not authorized to rely on this video as a source of legal advice. The use of this video does not create an attorney-client relationship between CLS and any user.

segments.text: Letters testamentary come down to three questions:
what they are, how to get them from the probate court, and how to use them once they
are issued.
Almost every institution in estate settlement asks to see this document first.
This video covers each part in order.
This video provides general information, not legal advice.
Probate rules vary by state and county.
For questions about a specific situation, contact the local probate court or a
licensed attorney.
Four points explain what this document is.
The executor's credential. Despite the plural name, it is typically a single
court-issued document. They grant the executor named in a will the legal authority
to act for the estate.
Why institutions require them. Without letters, banks, title companies, and insurers
will not act. The purpose is protection:
only a court-authorized person can manage the estate.
Letters testamentary versus letters of administration.
Letters testamentary are issued when there is a valid will that names an executor.
Letters of administration are issued when there is no will, the will is invalid, or
the named executor cannot serve.
Both give the same practical authority.
When the named executor can't serve.
Only the person named in the will can petition for letters testamentary.
If that person cannot serve, the court may appoint an alternate named in the will,
or an administrator.
The process varies by state and county, but the steps are similar.
Step one: the original will and a certified death certificate.
Courts require the original will, not a photocopy.
If only a copy can be found, additional legal steps are required.
Step two: file a petition for probate in the county where the deceased lived.
The petition asks the court to admit the will and appoint the executor.
It lists the beneficiaries, heirs, and estate assets.
Step three: notify interested parties.
Most states require notice to beneficiaries and legal heirs, and in many cases a
published notice in a local newspaper.
Step four: the court hearing. The judge reviews the will, confirms notice, checks
for objections, and evaluates whether the executor is fit to serve.
Uncontested hearings are usually brief, and in some states the court may waive the
hearing for simple estates.
Step five: the letters are issued.
If the court is satisfied, it issues letters testamentary confirming the executor's
appointment and authority over the estate.
Once issued, the letters are put to work.
Order enough certified copies. A common recommendation is at least five to ten.
Some institutions keep the copy they receive.
Ordering extras at the time of issuance is easier than requesting more later.
What the letters authorize. They let the executor access bank accounts, transfer
real estate, file final tax returns, pay debts, and distribute assets.
They also cover life insurance payable to the estate, as opposed to a named
beneficiary.
Expiration and freshness. In some states, letters expire after a set period and must
be renewed. Even where they do not, some institutions will not accept letters more
than sixty to ninety days old. Updated letters can be requested from the court
clerk.
A common question: how long does it take to get letters testamentary?
It varies by state and court backlog.
In straightforward cases, letters may be issued within two to six weeks of filing.
Busier courts or contested cases can take several months.
The tasks that apply depend on the state, whether there is a will, and what assets
the estate holds.
SwiftProbate is probate task management software that builds a personalized task
list based on those details. It's free to start.
To recap. What they are: the court-issued credential that lets the executor act for
the estate.
How to get them: the original will, a petition, notice to interested parties, and a
hearing.
Using them: order certified copies, present them to institutions, and watch for
expiration. A full written guide is linked in the description.

metadata.shortDescription:
Unlock the power of automated, data-driven direct mail marketing for real estate professionals. In this video, we’ll reveal how Consumer Title Company (and your business too) can leverage Title ToolBox integration with PRINTgenie Dynamic Data to turn life-event triggers into fully automated marketing campaigns — no manual work, no spreadsheets, and no minimum orders.

🔍 What You’ll Learn:

How Title ToolBox plugs directly into PRINTgenie so your lists sync automatically. 
PRINTgenie

The difference between Dynamic Data (auto-sync nightly) vs Data Export (one-click import) modes. 
PRINTgenie

A breakdown of multi-touch drip campaigns including direct mail, text, and email — all triggered as soon as a life event hits. 
PRINTgenie

Why no minimums is a big win — send 1 or thousands, it doesn’t matter. 
PRINTgenie

How to set your farm area, choose lead types (probate, divorce, NOD, bankruptcy, etc.), and let the system do the rest. 
PRINTgenie

Real stories from agents who’ve turned this into passive lead generation while they “live life.” 
PRINTgenie

Why This Matters for You / Your Clients

No more exporting, cleaning, or uploading lists manually. The system maps, cleans (USPS-validated), and activates campaigns automatically. 
PRINTgenie

Multi-channel outreach means higher deliverability and consistent brand touches across mail, text, email.

You don’t need to commit to large runs — no minimums means more flexibility and less risk.

Works 24/7: even while you sleep, marketing is being delivered.

Perfect for realtors, investors, title reps, or any business targeting motivated seller leads via life events.

🚀 Ready to Automate Your Marketing?

Visit www.PRINTgenie.io/dynamic-data to see how the integration works.

Book a free demo and watch your marketing work while you live.

Get started with no minimums and set it & forget it marketing.

Don’t leave leads on the table — let data drive your marketing, so you can focus on closing.

#DirectMailAutomation #RealEstateMarketing #TitleToolBox #PRINTgenie #MultiTouchCampaigns #NoMinimums #LeadGeneration #LifeEventLeads #DataDrivenMarketing #AutomatedMarketing

metadata.title: Do I Pay Capital Gains on an Inherited House?
metadata.author: The Legacy Desk
metadata.shortDescription:
Inherited a house or investments? Federal tax law generally resets the basis of property that passes at death to its fair market value at the date of death, and that can go up or down. A gift during life generally keeps the giver's basis instead. This video follows one house along a timeline, using federal law and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) publications, and covers joint-owner spouses, community property on the IRS's list, what the rule doesn't cover, and the Form 706 consistency rule. A sale may still produce a taxable gain.

Companion page (the rules and sources from this video):
https://thelegacydeskhq.com/episodes/ep07-step-up-in-basis/

General education, not legal advice.

4:33 Which transfers count
5:16 Married owners: joint tenancy between spouses
6:18 Married owners: community property
7:13 What the reset doesn't cover
7:48 When a Form 706 is required

segments.text: Someone on Reddit said an attorney told them that heirs who get a house
through a transfer-on-death deed don't get a "stepped up" cost basis,
so capital gains on a future sale would be figured from what the owner
originally paid.
Their question: "Is this true?"
Another person, whose father had put the house in their name but kept
the use of it for life,
asked whether they'd owe capital gains,
or whether "some kind of step up basis" applied to a sale.
Both come down to one question:
which number counts, what the parent paid,
or what the house was worth when the parent died?
To answer it, we'll follow one house along a timeline,
from the day it's bought to the day an heir sells it,
using federal tax law and Internal Revenue Service publications.
This is general education, not legal advice.
Talk to a licensed attorney in your state.
Stop one: the purchase.
Here's a made-up example, with made-up numbers:
a parent buys a house for one hundred thousand dollars.
Federal law says the basis of property is generally its cost,
so that starting figure is the parent's basis,
and basis matters when the property is sold.
Federal law says the gain on a sale is the amount realized minus
the adjusted basis, and a loss is the adjusted basis minus the amount realized.
So "which number counts" is really a question about basis.
Now jump ahead to the parent's death.
Federal law says the basis of property acquired from someone who has died
is generally its fair market value at the date of death.
That includes property passed through a will or inheritance.
It also includes property the person put in a trust during life,
if they kept the income for life and the right,
at all times before death, to revoke the trust.
And the IRS says this basis rule applies whether or not the executor files
Form 706, the federal return for the tax on transfers at death.
For an inherited home, IRS Publication 523 says your basis is the fair market
value on the date of death,
or on a later alternate valuation date if the personal representative chose one.
In our made-up example, the house is worth four hundred thousand dollars when
the parent dies, so that becomes the heir's basis.
If this is helping, subscribing gets you the next real question.
Next stop: the heir sells.
Gain is measured from that reset basis,
not from what the parent paid.
In the made-up example, a sale for four hundred ten thousand dollars would show
a gain of about ten thousand,
in a simplified version that ignores selling costs and improvements.
That gain may still be taxable,
because selling for more than your basis gives a taxable gain.
Inherited property is also treated as held for more than a year,
even if it's sold within a year of the death.
And the reset works both ways:
it's a step-up, or a step-down.
If the house was worth less at the date of death than the parent
paid, the heir's basis is generally that lower value.
Now rewind the timeline and take the other branch:
the parent, still alive, gives the house to the child.
Federal law says property received as a gift generally keeps the giver's basis.
There's one twist: if the giver's basis is higher than the fair market value
at the time of the gift,
that lower value is used for figuring a loss.
In the made-up example, the child's basis stays at one hundred thousand dollars,
so the same four hundred ten thousand dollar sale would show a gain
of about three hundred ten thousand,
in the same simplified version.
That's the difference between the two branches,
and it's why "put the house in the kids' names now" can change
the tax picture.
A tax professional can tell you whether either path fits a particular family.
So which transfers at death get the reset?
Besides wills, inheritance and that kind of revocable trust,
federal law also treats property as acquired from the person who died if
it passes because of their death or the form of ownership and has
to be included in their gross estate for the federal tax on transfers at
death.
That's what the two questions from the start turn on.
Whether a transfer-on-death deed, or a deed where the parent keeps the use
of the house for life, meets that test depends on rules our sources
for this episode don't cover.
So we won't answer either question here.
A tax professional can tell you whether that test is met for a particular
deed.
Now say a married couple owns the same house together,
and one spouse dies first.
If the spouses were the only joint owners,
as joint tenants with right of survivorship or as tenants by the entirety,
federal law includes one-half of the value in the first spouse's gross estate.
It doesn't matter how much each spouse paid or which spouse dies first.
IRS Publication 551 says the surviving spouse's basis is the cost of their own
half, with certain adjustments, plus their basis in the half they inherited.
So only the inherited half resets;
the survivor's own half keeps its cost.
That half rule applies only when the spouses are the only joint owners,
and it generally doesn't apply if the surviving spouse isn't a United States
citizen.
Community property works differently.
The IRS lists Arizona, California, Idaho,
Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington and Wisconsin as community property
states.
The IRS says that when a spouse dies,
the total value of the community property,
even the surviving spouse's part, generally becomes the basis of the entire
property.
For that to apply, at least half the value of the community property interest
has to be includible in the estate of the spouse who died,
for the federal tax on transfers at death,
whether or not a return has to be filed.
Whether a particular asset counts as community property is a question of state law
that this episode doesn't cover.
Here are two things that fall outside the reset.
First, the rule doesn't apply to property that's a right to receive what
the tax code calls "income in respect of a decedent".
What counts as that is a question for a tax professional.
Second, a gift that comes back.
If someone gives appreciated property to a person who dies within one year,
and it comes back to the giver or the giver's spouse,
the basis is the adjusted basis of the person who died,
just before death, not the value at death.
One more stop applies only when a Form 706 had to be filed
for the person who died.
Then the executor must file Form 8971 and give a Schedule A to certain
beneficiaries, though there are exceptions.
For property whose inclusion increased the tax owed on that return,
the heir's basis can't be more than its final value for that tax.
IRS Publication 544 says that if your Schedule A shows the property increased
that tax, you use a basis consistent with that final value.
And the IRS warns that an accuracy-related penalty may apply if someone reporting
the sale of certain inherited property uses a basis above that final value.
That consistency rule applies only to property whose inclusion increased the tax.
So what's worth gathering along the way?
For the value on the date of death,
the IRS says you can contact the executor.
If property came as a gift,
the IRS says you need the giver's adjusted basis,
the value at the time of the gift,
and any gift tax paid.
And if a Schedule A arrives,
it matters for your basis.
Before selling or giving property away,
a tax professional can tell you whether the reset applies and what your basis
is.
So, back to the question: which number counts?
When property passes at death in one of the ways federal law lists,
generally the value at the date of death,
up or down, not what the parent paid.
When it's a gift during life,
generally the giver's basis carries over.
A sale may still produce a taxable gain either way.
And whether either of those two deeds qualifies is the question we've left
for a professional.
General education, not legal advice.
This doesn't create an attorney–client relationship.
Questions about these rules?
Leave them in the comments.
Next time: when what someone leaves behind is small enough that full probate might
not be needed.
This has been The Legacy Desk.
Thanks for watching.

📞 Free 15-minute call, no pressure: https://triciagarcia.com/calendar

Selling an inherited home can feel overwhelming — siblings start arguing, families panic, and people often make emotional decisions that cost them thousands in taxes. But here’s the part most families never hear from their CPA: the step-up basis often eliminates your taxable gain entirely.

📖 Read the full breakdown, with IRS sources, the documents you need, and step-up vs. Prop 19: https://leisurevillagelife.com/step-up-in-basis-inherited-home/

In this video, I break down exactly how the tax rules work when you inherit a home, why selling at the wrong time can trigger unnecessary taxes, and the crucial appraisal step that helped my client legally owe $0 after selling their parents’ property.

You’ll learn:
✅ What the step-up basis really means
✅ Why sale price vs. date-of-death value matters
✅ Why some families pay taxes they never actually owed
✅ How an appraisal can save you $40,000 or more
✅ Common mistakes when selling inherited property

If you inherited a home in Ventura County, LA County, or anywhere in California, this video will help you avoid costly mistakes and understand the process clearly — without the confusion, fear, or pressure.

📲 Have questions about your inherited home or need guidance?
Schedule a call with me here:  https://realestatetoolbox.com/bookacall

🏡 Serving Ventura County, LA County & nationwide through referral partnerships (outside the area? https://triciagarcia.com/agent-referral). I help families navigate inherited homes, senior transitions, probate sales, and major real estate decisions with clarity and compassion.

metadata.title: Step Up in Basis Real Estate: Sell Now or Hold Until Death? (2026)
metadata.author: Hans Goldstein: Tax & Exit Planning
metadata.shortDescription:
Under IRC Section 1014, property that passes at death gets a new income tax basis equal to its fair market value on the date of death.
Full page: https://bigsaletax.com/tools/step-up-at-death-hold/

Free 2026 tax sheets: https://bigsaletax.com/

A California married couple filing jointly sells $5 million of land with a $1 million basis for cash in 2026, and the site's tax engine shows a total added tax of $1,442,169. If they hold the land until death instead, the heirs' basis under IRC section 1014 becomes $5 million, so that tax is gone rather than deferred, but holding means giving up the cash during life and risking a lower value at death.

Sources named on the page (page last reviewed October 3, 2026): IRC 1014 (Cornell LII); IRC 691 (Cornell LII); IRC 2010 (Cornell LII); IRC 2040 (Cornell LII); IRC 469 (Cornell LII); IRC 6035 (Cornell LII); Rev. Rul. 2023-2 (IRS); About Form 8971 (IRS)

Education only. Not tax, legal or financial advice. Tax law changes; every rate and limit in this video is dated and sourced on screen and on the linked page, which is the current source. Narration is an AI audio overview (NotebookLM) generated from the page; every sentence was checked against the page and anything that did not match was cut.

Produced with AI tools from Hans Goldstein's research.

WHEN A PARENT NEEDS CARE AND THERE’S A HOME INVOLVED

Dale Corpus helps families navigate senior care decisions - especially when a home is involved.

As a Senior Transition Strategist, Realtor, and Reverse Mortgage Specialist, Dale helps families evaluate their options when care, housing, and finances intersect.

Whether you’re considering senior living, aging in place, selling a home to fund care, or using a reverse mortgage to remain at home, families often have more options than they realize. You don’t have to figure it out alone.

START HERE - Personalized Guidance + Resources
 Explore resources, ask questions using the AI Resource Explorer, or connect with Dale directly:
 https://www.simplifyseniortransitions.com/starthere

CARE FUNDING CALCULATOR
 Estimate how income, assets, and home equity may help pay for senior care:
 https://www.simplifyseniortransitions.com/care-funding-calculator

PODCAST EPISODE LIBRARY
 Browse conversations with senior living experts, elder law attorneys, home care leaders, financial professionals, and families navigating these decisions every day:
 https://www.simplifyseniortransitions.com/podcastlibrary

Selling a Parent’s Home in the Bay Area — What Families Need to Know

Helping your aging parent transition to senior living isn’t just about selling a home — it’s navigating a legal, financial, and emotional maze. 🧭

In this new episode of the Simplify Senior Transitions Podcast, I break down what every Bay Area family should know before listing a senior’s home, including:

✅ Legal must-knows — power of attorney, title issues, and probate
💰 Smart financial planning — funding care and managing tax implications
💙 Handling the emotional side — family disagreements, downsizing, and letting go

If you’re supporting an aging loved one in Contra Costa, Alameda, Santa Clara, San Mateo, San Francisco, Solano, or Napa County, this one’s for you.

Don’t wait for a crisis — plan ahead with clarity and compassion.

segments.text: Ready to turn a house into a home for
seniors and a gold mine for you? In
today's video, I'm spilling the secrets
to starting a residential assisted
living business that checks all the
boxes and the bank accounts.
Requirements and regulations for
assisted living homes vary
state-tostate. So, it's important to
start by familiarizing yourself with the
local laws and your state's health
department guidelines to avoid costly
delays or penalties during the licensing
process. Next, create a well-thoughtout
business plan that outlines your goals,
target market, pricing, services, and
your financial projections. Decide
whether you're going to offer general
assisted living, or focused on memory
care, specialized care for residents
with dementia. Keep your startup costs
in mind as they may include purchasing,
you know, real estate or purchasing land
and building real estate or renovating a
property, obtaining necessary licenses,
hiring staff, FFN, carrying costs, and
marketing your business. Additionally,
you'll need to plan for ongoing expenses
like utilities, insurance, and employee
salaries, which will take up 40% of your
total expenses. A clear business plan
will not only help you stay organized,
but it's also essential if you plan to
get financing from a bank or an
investor, which I highly recommend you
do. Do not use your own money for this.
When choosing a location, look for
somewhere that's safe, accessible, and
appealing to potential residents and
their families. If you plan to convert
an existing single family home, be sure
that it can meet zoning requirements and
state regulations for assisted living
facilities. Renovations may be necessary
to add safety features and expand living
spaces or create communal areas. Keep in
mind that the design and comfort of your
home will directly impact its appeal. As
someone's walking through, if it doesn't
feel good, they're not going to choose
you, and that will directly impact your
success. Once your property is ready,
it's time to put your focus on staffing.
Hiring qualified and compassionate staff
is really important since you know
they're going to be the ones directly
caring for the residents, not you.
Caregivers should meet state training
requirements and have experience in
elder care. You'll also need to hire a
licensed administrator to run all the
day-to-day within the home. Beyond
technical qualifications, you're going
to want to hire people who are
empathetic, patient, and committed to
providing highquality care. Proper
training and ongoing professional
development are going to be crucial to
maintaining a skilled and motivated
team. Especially if you want people who
are going to do the job well when you're
not there. You know, if you're serious
about opening an RAL home, you're not
going to learn it all in one short
video. We actually host 3day trainings
in Phoenix, Arizona, where we break it
down step by step by step how you can do
this in any market. Consider coming out
to Phoenix, Arizona for one of our
upcoming trainings. Or watch this video
right here on YouTube for the next most
important steps to take. Marketing is
going to play a big role in the success
of your business. If you don't market,
you won't fill your beds and you're not
going to have a business. So, make sure
you build a professional website that
highlights your services, mission, and
amenities. Include photos of your
facility and videos if you can, and
clear contact information. Who are you?
How do they get in touch with you?
Eventually, you'll want to add
testimonials from residents and their
families. And word of mouth
recommendations are really going to be a
powerful marketing tool for you.
Networking with local health care
providers like geriatric doctors, elder
law attorneys, senior centers, placement
agents, and community organizations can
help you gain referrals, but you may
have to pay for those leads. as well as
hosting open houses and facility tours.
This can really help you showcase, you
know, what makes your home special. When
they walk inside and they can feel the
energy and the environment, they'll
surely be able to tell if it's right for
them or not. Finally, focus on
delivering excellent care and
maintaining compliance with state
regulations. Regular inspections are
common in the assisted living industry,
so staying organized and proactive about
meeting safety and standard care is a
must. Beyond compliance, you need to
prioritize creating a warm and welcoming
environment for your residents. Offer
engaging activities, nutritious meals,
and personalized care plans to enhance
their quality of life. Keep in mind that
when your residents are happy and well
cared for, your reputation will blossom,
and this is going to lead to higher
occupancy rates and long-term success.
If you want to join our mission to
positively impact 10 million seniors
with residential assisted living, be
sure to subscribe to this channel right

metadata.title: How to Buy Out Your Siblings When You Inherit a House (Ontario)
metadata.author: Michelle Bell - Realtor
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to keep your parents' house, but your siblings want their share of the inheritance? Here's how buying out your siblings works in Ontario, what it could cost and what you need to know before making an agreement.

Inheriting a family home can be complicated, especially when one sibling wants to keep the house and the others would rather sell.

The good news? If you've inherited a share of the property, that share may help you finance the buyout. You may not need to borrow the full market value of the home.

In this episode of Sandwiched, I'm walking you through five things to consider when buying out your siblings after inheriting a house in Ontario.

We'll cover:

• How to start the conversation with your siblings and the executor

• How to determine a fair market value for an inherited home

• How to calculate a sibling buyout using a $900,000 house

• Whether your inherited share can count as equity toward financing

• What happens when there's still a mortgage on the property

• Legal fees, possible taxes and other costs to consider

• Why you need a written agreement before moving forward

• What happens if your siblings don't agree to the buyout

For example, if three siblings inherit a $900,000 mortgage-free house equally, the sibling keeping the property may need to fund the other two siblings' $600,000 combined shares, plus applicable costs.

But every estate is different. Existing mortgages, debts, taxes, the will and lender requirements can all affect how a buyout works.

🏡 FREE PARENTS' HOUSE PLAYBOOK

Dealing with your parents' house or helping them plan for the future?

I've created a free guide covering inherited property in Ontario, probate, executor responsibilities and the options for keeping, renting or selling the family home.

Download your free guide:
https://sandwiched.ca/

ABOUT SANDWICHED

I'm Michelle Bell, a Realtor since 2009, serving Georgetown, Halton Hills, Oakville and the Greater Toronto Area.

Sandwiched is where we talk about our parents, our kids, the houses, the money and the decisions that come with being caught between generations.

From helping your kids buy their first home to navigating inheritance, downsizing parents and protecting family equity, we're having the conversations that matter.

Explore more real estate resources:
https://michellebell.ca/

Subscribe for more videos about inherited houses, family real estate decisions and generational wealth in Canada.

Real estate, redefined for real life.

This video is for general information and does not replace individual legal, tax or mortgage advice. Have the appropriate professionals review your situation.

#InheritedHouse #BuyingOutSiblings #OntarioRealEstate #Sandwiched #InheritanceCanada

metadata.title: 6 Critical First Steps if You Just Inherited a House
metadata.author: Sell That Wreck! With Stephanie Burt
metadata.shortDescription:
If you just inherited a house, you're probably wondering where to even begin. Before you make any decisions about selling, renovating, or keeping the property, there are critical steps that need to happen first — and most people don't know about all of them.

In this video, I walk you through exactly what to do when you inherit a house, including how to protect a vacant property, what your homeowner's insurance may not be covering, how to find out what the property really owes beyond the mortgage, and how to avoid the mistakes that cost heirs thousands of dollars before they ever list the house. Whether you're dealing with an inherited house that needs work, an estate property full of belongings, or multiple heirs who need to get aligned — this checklist covers everything you need to know before you make your next move.

0:00 - The "Not So Obvious" List of What To Do
0:30 - Step 1 - Utilities & Homeowners Insurance
1:59 - Step 2 - Police Watch & Crawlspace
2:41 - Step 3 - Get a Probate Attorney Early
3:23 - Step 4 - What Does The House Owe? 
4:03 - Step 5 - Get All Heirs On The Same Page
5:02 - How To Get Help
5:31 - Step 6 - The Belongings
7:05 - Your Ready for the Next Phase 
7:25 - Ask Me Anything

👉 Free PDF - https://www.stephburtcashoffers.com/6-steps-you-must-do-when-you-inherit-a-house/

🔔 Subscribe for weekly real estate insight from both sides of the market — agent and investor.

🏠 Stuck with a property you can't deal with right now? I’ll walk you through your options - cash offer, listing or both: 
You can reach me here:
👉 Work With Me (Metro Atlanta):
https://www.stephburtcashoffers.com

👉 Ask Me Anything (totally anonymous):
https://www.stephburtcashoffers.com/ask-me-anything/

DISCLAIMER: I am a licensed realtor and real estate investor, not an attorney or accountant. Always consult qualified professionals for legal and tax advice.

#InheritedHouse #InheritedProperty #EstateProperty #SellingInheritedHome #ProbateRealEstate #AtlantaRealEstate #RealEstateTips #HouseFlipping #AtlantaHomesBurt #WhatToDoWithInheritedHouse

Selling an inherited home can involve more than getting the property ready for the market. If you're an executor, administrator, or trustee, knowing what to handle first can make the process easier to manage.

In this video, Kim Ward shares 10 steps to take before listing a loved one's home, from confirming your authority and securing the property to reviewing insurance, managing personal belongings, planning repairs, and keeping beneficiaries informed.

Every property and estate is different, but having a plan can help you stay organized as you prepare for the sale.
