A tenant who pays on time, takes reasonable care of the property, and follows the lease agreement can make a landlord's life considerably easier. A tenant who stops paying rent, damages the property, or creates legal disputes can turn an apparently profitable investment into an expensive problem. That's why tenant screening is an important part of rental property management. Landlords commonly review rental applications, verify income, check rental history, and evaluate credit and background information where legally permitted. They may also contact previous landlords to understand whether an applicant paid rent reliably and respected lease conditions. But screening isn't simply about finding the person with the highest salary. Landlords must follow federal, state, and local fair housing laws. Decisions cannot be based on protected characteristics, and tenant screening policies should be consistent and legally compliant. Once a tenant is approved, the landlord and tenant generally sign a lease agreement. The lease defines the rent, payment dates, security deposit arrangements, responsibilities, property rules, and other important conditions. It also establishes the legal relationship between the two parties. And here's something many first-time investors underestimate. A landlord is not simply renting out a building. They're operating a service business. The property must be maintained. Tenant concerns must be addressed. Repairs must be organized. Legal obligations must be followed. Even if the landlord hires a management company, someone still has to make decisions about the property. This is why some investors prefer professional property management. A property manager can advertise vacant units, communicate with tenants, coordinate contractors, collect rent, and help manage the day-to-day operation. But these services are not free. Management fees reduce the investor's income, and additional fees may apply for tenant placement, lease renewals, inspections, or specific maintenance services. Some landlords manage their own properties to reduce expenses. Others decide their time is more valuable than the management fee. Neither approach is automatically better. The decision depends on how many properties they own, how far away they live, how much time they have, and how comfortable they are dealing with tenants and maintenance. Now let's talk about one of the biggest reasons rental property investors are interested in real estate in the first place, the mortgage. Remember Michael's $280,000 mortgage? Every monthly payment contains two important components, interest and principle. Interest is the cost of borrowing money. Principle is the amount that reduces the outstanding loan balance. At the beginning of a traditional fixed-rate mortgage, a relatively large portion of the monthly payment goes toward interest. Over time, as the outstanding balance declines, more of each payment goes toward principle. This process is called amortization. And here's where the long-term strategy becomes interesting. Suppose Michael keeps the property for several years. His tenant continues paying rent, and the rental income helps cover the mortgage. As Michael makes mortgage payments, the outstanding loan balance gradually decreases. He is building equity. Equity is the difference between the property's market value and the amount still owed on the mortgage. Imagine the house is worth $350,000 and Michael owes $270,000 on the mortgage. His equity is approximately $80,000. If the property value rises while the mortgage balance falls, his equity can grow from two different directions. This is one of the most powerful features of real estate investing. However, equity is not the same as spendable cash. Michael cannot automatically use that equity to pay his everyday bills. He would generally need to sell the property, refinance, or obtain another form of financing to access it. And each option has costs and risks. Refinancing can involve closing costs, new interest rates, and a larger loan balance. Selling can involve agent commissions, closing costs, taxes, and the repayment of the remaining mortgage. So equity is valuable, but investors must understand how and when they can access it. Now let's consider appreciation. Property appreciation means an increase in the market value of real estate over time. A house might become more valuable because of rising demand, new infrastructure, population growth, improvements to the neighborhood, or broader changes in the housing market. But appreciation is never guaranteed. Property values can stagnate or decline. Interest rates can rise, reducing the number of buyers who can afford homes. Local employers can leave. Insurance premiums can increase. Neighborhood conditions can change. An investor who depends entirely on appreciation may discover that the investment does not produce the financial results they expected. That's why experienced investors try to evaluate a property based on its current economics, not just on what they hope it will be worth 10 years from now. And this brings us to another essential part of the business, preparing for unexpected expenses. A rental property needs an emergency reserve. A roof replacement, HVAC failure, plumbing emergency, damage, or extended vacancy can create expenses that are much larger than the monthly maintenance budget. If Michael has no cash reserves, one unexpected repair could force him to borrow money or sell the property at the wrong time. A responsible investor plans for these possibilities before purchasing. The exact reserve amount depends on the property's age, condition, insurance, local repair costs, financing, and vacancy risk. But the principle is straightforward. Never assume that every dollar collected in rent is available to spend. Some of that money belongs to the property's future expenses. Now let's examine one of the most discussed advantages of rental property investing. Taxes. Rental property owners may be able to deduct eligible business expenses against rental income, subject to applicable tax rules. These expenses can include mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, maintenance, repairs, management fees, and other qualifying costs. But one of the most interesting tax concepts is depreciation. In the United States, residential rental buildings are generally depreciated over 27.5 years under the applicable tax rules, while land itself is not depreciable. Depreciation is a non-cash expense for tax purposes. That means an investor may receive rental income while also claiming an annual depreciation deduction, even though they aren't necessarily spending that amount of cash during the year. This can reduce taxable rental income. However, depreciation rules are complicated. The property must meet the applicable requirements, and depreciation may affect taxes when the property is sold. Depreciation recapture can apply, and the tax treatment depends on the investor's circumstances. This is why rental property owners often work with qualified tax professionals. The goal isn't simply to collect rent. It's to understand how rental income, deductible expenses, depreciation, financing, and future sale taxes interact. And once an investor understands these fundamentals, a new possibility emerges, scaling. Michael started with one property, but imagine that over time he improves his finances, builds savings, and purchases another rental property, then another. Instead of depending on a single tenant, he now has multiple tenants generating rental income across several properties. This creates diversification within his real estate portfolio, although it does not eliminate market risk. Owning five properties doesn't automatically make someone wealthy. If every property has negative cash flow, expensive debt, and major maintenance requirements, owning more properties can simply multiply the problems. The goal is not to collect as many houses as possible. The goal is to own properties whose economics make sense. Some investors use a strategy known as BRRRR. The letters stand for buy, rehab, rent, refinance, and repeat. The basic idea is to purchase a property that needs improvement, renovate it, rent it out, refinance based on its new value and lending conditions, and potentially use some of the recovered capital toward another investment. For example, an investor might purchase a distressed property below market value, spend money renovating it, and then rent it to a tenant. If the renovation increases the property's appraised value, the investor may be able to refinance and recover part of the capital invested. But BRRRR is not a guaranteed money-making machine. Renovations can exceed the budget, appraisals can come in lower than expected, interest rates can change, lenders may have stricter requirements, and the property may not rent for the expected amount. The strategy depends on buying correctly, controlling renovation costs, and having a realistic financing plan. And this brings us to the risks that can turn a real estate portfolio into a financial burden. The first major risk is excessive debt. Leverage can increase returns, but it also increases financial pressure. A landlord with highly leveraged properties may struggle if rental income falls or interest and operating costs increase. The second risk is vacancy. If tenants leave and properties remain empty, mortgage payments and operating expenses continue. The third risk is unexpected maintenance. A single major repair can consume months of rental income. The fourth risk is falling property values. An investor who needs to sell during a weak market may have to accept a loss. The fifth risk is changing local conditions. A new apartment development can increase competition. A major employer closing can reduce housing demand. Insurance costs and property taxes can rise. These risks are why real estate investing requires more than optimism. It requires financial discipline, research, and a margin of safety. History offers an important reminder. During the 2008 financial crisis, the American housing market experienced a dramatic collapse. Home prices fell in many areas. Foreclosures increased. Mortgage markets came under severe pressure, and many homeowners and investors suffered enormous financial losses. Some investors had purchased properties with too much debt and too little financial protection. When property values fell and financing became difficult, they discovered that real estate does not always move upward. The lesson is not that real estate is a bad investment. The lesson is that leverage, poor underwriting, and excessive risk can turn a promising investment into a financial disaster. And not everyone who wants exposure to rental real estate wants to become a landlord. This is where real estate investment trusts, or REITs, enter the picture. A REIT is a company that owns, operates, or finances income-producing real estate and generally allows investors to purchase shares in the business. Instead of buying an entire rental house, an investor can buy shares of a publicly traded REIT through a brokerage account. Some REITs own apartment buildings. Others own shopping centers, office buildings, warehouses, healthcare facilities, or other types of property. For example, Realty Income is known for its large portfolio of commercial properties and its monthly dividend payments. Equity Residential is known for owning and operating apartment properties in major American markets. These companies provide a way to participate in real estate without personally finding tenants, arranging repairs, or managing individual buildings. But REITs have their own risks. Their share prices can fluctuate. Interest rates can affect valuations and borrowing costs. Property markets can weaken, and dividends are not guaranteed. And unlike directly owning a rental property, investors in publicly traded REITs do not personally control the underlying buildings. So which approach is better? Direct ownership offers control, the possibility of using mortgage leverage, and direct responsibility for the property's operations. REITs offer liquidity, diversification, and access to real estate without the everyday responsibilities of being a landlord. The right choice depends on an investor's goals, available capital, risk tolerance, and willingness to manage property. Technology is also changing the rental property business. Online platforms make it easier to advertise vacancies, collect rent, screen applicants, and communicate with tenants. Property management software can help landlords track expenses, organize maintenance requests, and monitor the financial performance of multiple properties. Smart home devices can help monitor temperature, leaks, and security. Data tools can help investors compare rental markets, estimate expenses, and evaluate potential properties. But technology cannot remove the fundamental economics. A property still needs tenants. Rent still needs to cover expenses. Debt still needs to be repaid. And unexpected problems can still happen. Now let's return to Michael. He started with $90,000 in savings and the dream of owning a rental property. He discovered that a $350,000 house generating $2,500 in monthly rent could still lose money after expenses and mortgage payments. He learned that a beautiful property is not necessarily a profitable property. He learned that cash flow, net operating income, cap rate, cash on cash return, mortgage amortization, equity, appreciation, taxes, and risk all matter. And perhaps most importantly, he learned that the purchase price determines much of the investment's future financial potential. If Michael wants to build a successful portfolio, he may need to negotiate a lower purchase price, find a property with stronger rental income, reduce financing costs, or identify ways to operate the property more efficiently. He may also decide that the first property simply isn't the right investment. Walking away from a bad deal can be a better financial decision than forcing a purchase because real estate investing is not about owning a property at any cost. It's about making the numbers work. And when the numbers work, rental property can create several potential sources of financial return. There can be monthly cash flow, there can be mortgage principal reduction, there can be property appreciation, there can be certain tax advantages, and there can be opportunities to use accumulated equity to finance future investments. But none of these benefits is automatic. Every property has its own economics, and every investor has to evaluate the risks. A rental property is not a savings account. It is not guaranteed passive income. It is a real business built around a physical asset, a financing structure, a local housing market, and the people who pay to live there. The most successful investors understand this before they buy. They don't fall in love with the house. They study the numbers. They don't assume that rising property values will rescue a bad investment. They build reserves. They don't treat rent as profit. They calculate what remains after every expense. And they understand that wealth in real estate is often built through patience, disciplined purchasing, responsible debt management, and long-term ownership. Because the real secret of rental property investing isn't simply owning more houses, it's understanding what each house actually earns, what it really costs, and how much risk you're taking to own it. And sometimes, the smartest real estate investment isn't the property you buy. It's the expensive mistake you decide not to make. Like, subscribe.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning Rental Properties (The Hidden Costs That Eat Your Profits!)
metadata.author: Unit Math
metadata.shortDescription:
What does it really cost to own rental properties in 2026? The idea sounds simple: buy a house, collect rent, pay the mortgage, and keep the profit. But the real economics of rental property investing are much more complicated.

In this video, we break down the numbers behind a $300,000 rental property earning $2,400 per month. We examine operating expenses, mortgage payments, property taxes, insurance, maintenance, vacancy, cash flow, and appreciation to discover how much a landlord actually makes.

You'll also learn why a property with a 10% gross rental yield can produce only a 5.4% cap rate—and why rising interest rates can turn a profitable rental into a monthly loss.

We cover:
- The real operating costs of owning rental properties
- How mortgage rates affect rental cash flow
- Cap rates and negative leverage
- Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR)
- Cash flow vs. appreciation
- Why older landlords may have a major financing advantage
- Property taxes, insurance, and maintenance risks
- Managing a 10-property rental portfolio
- Real estate depreciation and tax considerations

**The numbers behind our example:**
- Property price: $300,000
- Monthly rent: $2,400
- Gross rental yield: 10%
- Cap rate: approximately 5.4%
- Mortgage interest rate: 7.75%
- Annual cash flow: approximately -$3,100
- Debt Service Coverage Ratio: 0.84

The biggest lesson? Rent is revenue. What remains after every expense and loan payment is what really matters.

This video is for educational purposes only and is not financial, tax, or legal advice. Figures are illustrative.

A 10% gross yield became a 5 and 1/2% real yield. than 40% of the rent disappeared before the owner saw a dollar. One 2026 analysis found that for typical priced homes, the net yield after taxes, insurance, vacancy, repairs and management is often only 1 to 2%. Ours is on the better end. The loan is $225,000 at 7 and 3/4% a typical 2026 rate for an investment property on a 30-year fixed loan. The monthly payment of principal and interest is about $1,612. That's about $19,340 a year. Now compare. The house earns $16,176. The loan costs $19,342. The landlord is losing about $3,100 a year and that's before the owner has paid for anything unexpected. This is called negative leverage. It happens when the property's cap rate, 5.4% is lower than the cost of the loan, 7 and 3/4. Every dollar borrowed earns less than it costs. Rent has to rise as much as the payment does and at 1.8% a year it takes years to catch up. There's another problem and it comes from the lender. Investor lenders look at a ratio called the debt service coverage ratio. The property's NOI divided by the yearly loan payment. They usually want it to be at least about 1.2. metadata.title: How Do You Determine the Right Asking Price for a Probate Property? | California Probate
metadata.author: Matt McGilvray
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you determine the right asking price when selling a probate property in California?

Pricing a probate home involves more than looking at recent neighborhood sales. The property's condition, comparable sales, necessary repairs, current market conditions, and the type of probate authority can all affect the pricing strategy.

In this video, we discuss why setting a realistic asking price matters and how executors and administrators can approach this important decision.

Whether you're considering selling a probate property as-is or making improvements before listing, understanding its market value is an important first step.

Matt McGilvray
Broker Associate | RE/MAX New Dimension
Certified Probate and Trust Specialist

Serving Riverside, San Bernardino, Orange, and Los Angeles Counties.

Call or text: 714-318-4237

segments.text: How do you determine the right asking
price for a probate property?
It's one of the most important decisions
an executor or administrator will make
when selling an inherited home.
Price it too high and the property could
sit on the market for months. Price it
too low and the estate could leave money
on the table.
I'm Matt McGilvray, broker associate
with RE/MAX New Dimension. In this
video, I'll explain the factors that
help determine a competitive asking
price for a probate property in Southern
California.
Determining the right asking price for a
probate property involves more than
simply looking at what nearby homes are
listed for. I start by reviewing recent
comparable sales, focusing on properties
similar in size, location, age, and
features.
Next, I evaluate the property's
condition.
Does it need major repairs, cosmetic
improvements, or is it ready for a buyer
to move in?
I also consider the probate appraisal,
which may differ from what buyers are
willing to pay in today's market.
Finally, I look at current market
conditions, including competing
listings, buyer demand, and how long
similar homes are taking to sell.
Together, these factors help establish a
realistic asking price designed to
attract qualified buyers and protect the
estate's value.
One question I frequently hear from
executors is, should we list the
property at the probate referee's
appraised value?
Not necessarily.
In California, probate referees
typically don't visit the property.
Instead, they rely on public records,
comparable sales, online valuation
tools, and other available information.
That means they may not know whether the
home has been beautifully remodeled,
needs significant repairs, or has
serious condition issues.
The probate appraisal serves
purpose in administering the estate, but
it isn't necessarily the price a buyer
will pay. That's why I personally
evaluate the property's condition,
review recent comparable sales, and
analyze current market conditions before
recommending an asking price. The goal
is to establish a realistic price that
reflects what buyers are willing to pay
in today's market.
Here's something every executor and
administrator should understand when
pricing a probate property in
California, the 90% rule.
When a probate sale requires court
confirmation, the court generally cannot
approve a sale for less than 90% of the
property's appraised value.
For example, if the probate referee
values a home at $800,000,
the minimum sale price generally must be
at least $720,000.
But here's an important distinction. The
90% rule doesn't tell us what the home
is worth in today's real estate market
or what we should list it for.
And not every probate sale requires
court confirmation. Many personal
representatives have full authority
under the Independent Administration of
Estates Act, allowing them to sell
without a confirmation hearing. That's
why understanding the type of probate
authority, the appraisal, and current
market conditions is essential before
establishing an asking price.
Even when the 90% rule doesn't legally
apply, the executor still has a
responsibility to obtain a reasonable
price and protect the estate's
interests.
One of the biggest mistakes when selling
a probate property is starting with an
asking price that's too high.
Some executors believe they can always
reduce the price later if the home
doesn't sell.
But the first few weeks on the market
are often when a property receives the
most attention from potential buyers.
If the asking price is unrealistic,
buyers may overlook the property
entirely.
And when a home sits on the market too
long, buyers may begin wondering what's
wrong with it.
The goal isn't to price the property as
high as possible. It's to establish a
competitive asking price that attracts
serious buyers, generates interest, and
helps the estate achieve the best
possible outcome. A well-supported
pricing strategy can make a significant
difference in how quickly and
successfully a probate property sells.
Questions about an inherited property?
Visit californiaprobaltyrealty.com
I'm Matt McGilvray with RE/MAX New
Dimension.
Experience and guidance when it matters
most.

metadata.title: What Every Probate Real Estate Specialist Needs to Know Before Making Probate Their Main Focus
metadata.author: Probate Mastery
metadata.shortDescription:
Being a probate real estate specialist brings a unique kind of pressure to the work we do every day.
When the market shifts, income feels uncertain.
When calls get emotional, the conversation carries weight.
When regulations change, both licensed and non licensed folks adjust right alongside the families they help.

Here’s where a probate real estate specialist stands out.
When the options you present feel clear and safe, families respond with trust.
When choices feel rushed or confusing, they pull back.

This coaching call walks through the conditions that help a probate business grow.
The same way real estate pros create movement by giving families choices that protect them and still support your work.

You will hear questions from agents, investors, wholesalers, and new professionals stepping into probate for the first time.
If you are building your foundation, the call gives direction.
If you are scaling, the call shows what to tighten so momentum stays steady.

Timestamps/Highlights :

00:00 What has to be done in setting up a well rounded business with probate
6:20 When you choose probate as your main thing, what makes it worth your time, energy, and money
16:20 For non license folks, what needs to be in place for you to feel confident that you get paid fairly when a lead chooses to list
24:30 What happens when probate becomes the core instead of a side option in your real estate business
37:50 What makes an option feel safe, practical, and respectful for heirs, and how to communicate those choices in a way that still supports your work
46:06 How do you decide which leads help your momentum and which ones slow you down

If these questions match what you deal with now, then this call helps you see your next move as a probate real estate specialist or someone entering the space.
If you want to understand how probate fits into your long term business, this conversation gives you a clear view of the path other professionals are taking.

Watch the call and notice which part connects with you first.
Your response usually points to your next step.

metadata.shortDescription:
In this coaching call, Bruce Hill breaks down the real models agents are using to build predictable probate pipelines, and more importantly, who each model is for.

Because the fastest way to drift in probate isn’t lack of effort.
It’s forcing yourself into a system that fights your personality, your schedule, or your stage of business.

Inside this session, you’ll see five proven approaches agents are running right now:

➡️ Referral-based partnerships for agents who value long-term trust and relationships
➡️ Mail-first models for those who prefer consistency over constant conversations
➡️ Call-forward strategies for agents who want speed and tighter feedback loops
➡️ Hybrid systems that blend mail and calls without overloading either
➡️ ISA-supported setups for teams ready to scale without losing control

As you watch, notice which model feels lighter to you.

Not which sounds impressive.
Not which someone else is using.
Which one feels sustainable with how you already think and work.

4:23 Different Business Models
How to tell which structure fits your current working style.

28:36 ISA Valuation & KPIs
What “fair and productive” really looks like when you scale support.

Why leading with service builds leverage you can’t buy.

metadata.shortDescription:
Richie had jury duty.
But instead of just checking in and leaving like everyone else…

He made one bold move.

He walked straight into the probate office with no script, no appointment just genuine curiosity and the desire to better serve his market.

30 minutes later, he walked out with:
- A crash course on the local probate process
-A working relationship with the courthouse clerk
- Names to circle prospect

Most real estate agents avoid the courthouse completely.
Or worse they walk in saying all the wrong things… and walk out with nothing.

Richie didn’t do anything complicated. He just led with service  . . .

Find out how Richie did it and hear the exact words he used in this snippet from one of our coaching calls

→ Start Building Your Probate Real Estate Expertise with Targeted Courses:

#probate #realestateleadgeneration #chadcorbett Probate Certification and Probate Training with Chad Corbett: Get off the real estate roller coaster and learn how to make more money in real estate.

Join our Facebook group, Estate Professionals Mastermind (more than a probate mastermind) https://facebook.com/groups/estateprofessionalsmastermind

The NAR 2021 Member Profile offers a picture of what the average real estate professional looks like:

Only one out of four earn $100,000 or more, and median gross income sits at $43,330.

Despite inflation, median income in this industry is DOWN 12.8% from $49,700 in 2019. 

So for the real estate agents and investors who are finding financial freedom, a happy work life balance, and a pathway to retiring early - How?  What's their methodology?

In this video, Chad Corbett lays out the most important advice anyone seeking answers on how to make money, build wealth, and achieve financial freedom through real estate needs to hear.

The best part? You can make it happen while loving what you do and helping hundreds of people along the way.

Is the Probate Niche and the Probate Mastery Certification Course right for me? https://probatemastery.com/warm-the-probate-solution/

Earn your certified probate real estate designation with 3 on-demand sessions, totaling 15 hours. Alumni receive the Certified Probate Expert (CPE) designation, access to weekly training calls with Chad Corbett, and an exclusive invitation to a Certified Probate Expert networking group. To learn more about Chad Corbett's probate course, read Probate Mastery reviews and see how they compare to MTI CPRES reviews, and enroll: https://probatemastery.com

metadata.title: What You Miss By Scrubbing Your Probate Real Estate Leads - Tips From Chad Corbett
metadata.author: All The Leads
metadata.shortDescription:
Get Certified in Probate: https://probatemastery.com

PROBATE LEADS: https://www.alltheleads.com/probate-leads

What You Miss By Scrubbing Your Probate Real Estate Leads - Probate Real Estate Deals That Aren't On Probate Property Lists!!!!

If you're reading this, it's probably because you're interested in probate real estate.  Whether you're already working your lead lists or just getting started, we've noticed something that agents, wholesalers, investors, brokers ALL do no matter how many times we share success stories from people who've done the opposite.
 
A lot of people make the mistake of scrubbing their lead lists down to  probate property lists.  The premise here is that scrubbing your lists will  maximize both your marketing budget and the time you spend cold calling probate leads.  In other words, why bother calling something if there is no property listed?

In this Tips From The Trainer Episode, Chad Corbett shares some big-ticket success stories to underscore the opportunity in every probate lead, whether the records indicate property in the estate or not!

6 Benefits of Not Scrubbing Your Probate Lists:
1) Better Contact Opportunities
2) Reach Family Members with more motivation, and possibly other real estate needs.
3) Referral Opportunities To Win Vendor Partnerships (when families need other services besides selling probate homes)
4) Lifelong Rapport - Provide a valuable service and warm introduction and you'll be top-of-mind for any future real estate needs.
5) Find Non-Probate Property - Not all property goes through probate!
6) Way Less Competition - Since everyone else is scrubbing their lead list.


 
People will tell you there's no property when there is. Court clerks and data researchers might leave an address out of the filing by error.  Probate might have been opened for any number of reasons, while property didn't need to go through the estate.  People inherit wealth they might want to invest in real estate. 

All of these situations have the potential to lead to listings, deals, and wholesale opportunities and your competition has passed them over.

Be the person that reaches out and establish connections with people from a place of value.  

Let another agent's mistake be your next deal!!!


Be sure to join our 24/7 Mastermind Group www.fb.com/groups/alltheleadsmastermind

For any questions about probate leads, mailbox motivator, ISA calling, credibility websites in your market visit https://my.alltheleads.com/checkmycounty or call 954-400-3500

Get 3 days of live training and a national Certified Probate Expert designation for just $250: https://alltheleads.com/education-training


#ProbateRealEstate #ColdCalling #WholesalingHouses #ProbateLeads

metadata.shortDescription:
Chad Corbett, founder of Probate Mastery and top probate coach, explains why probate calls are important. 

Sign up for Probate Mastery (affiliate link): https://courses.magnumopusproject.com/billgross

--
Bill Gross, The LAProbate Expert
I am a real estate broker in Los Angeles, CA focused on probate real estate and the leader of a team of over 1,100 agents nationally probate experts.

👉 Sign up for Probate Weekly to learn all about the probate real estate business: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/probate-weekly-tickets-272037841507

🔥 Join my Facebook Group to network with other professionals: https://www.facebook.com/groups/230687945401087

💸 Get Probate Cash with me on Wednesday mornings: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/get-probate-cash-tickets-420364640957 

➡️ Sign up for your FREE 1:1 call with me here: https://calendly.com/billgross/15min?month=2023-07 

Bill Gross is a licensed real estate broker in California (DRE 01022275) associated with EXP Realty, the Netflix of real estate. He is building a national network of probate-focused real estate agents. metadata.author: Probate Mastery
metadata.shortDescription:
You can start with mail or cold calling probate leads...what matters most is you know how to read timing and intent. 

In this clip, we break down how to combine calls and mail for better results.

You’ll learn how to use both strategies together instead of choosing one over the other:

✅ When to start with calls to qualify and build rapport
✅ When mail follow-ups create more trust and visibility
✅ How to read subtle cues that tell you a family is ready to move forward

This doesn’t mean cold calling is the only way...there are many ways to build consistent probate pipelines. What matters is knowing how to connect, listen, and move at the right pace. trust in probate.

Probate direct mail marketing can help real estate agents build consistent follow-up campaigns and stay in front of probate leads over time.

metadata.title: Probate Letters: How To Get These Magic Papers
metadata.author: American Estate Planning Series
metadata.shortDescription:
Build your estate plan online! MyAdvocate is the online solution for creating and maintaining your Will and all other legally-valid estate planning documents. Click the link below to get started!

https://www.myadvocate.com/join/paul

--

It's common when a family member attempts to handle the affairs of their deceased loved one, that the family member is told they cannot get any financial information of the deceased, and they certainly can't get access to frozen accounts without "Letters."

These "Letters" can be called many different things: Letters Testamentary, Letters of Administration, Letters of Independent Executorship, Letters of Independent Co-Administration, Letters from the Court, etc.

Think about it. Financial institutions cannot release financial information of a deceased customer just because a family members asks for it. And financial institutions certainly don't want the liability that comes from releasing a deceased's funds to the wrong person or people.

When someone dies with a Last Will that names an executor, the executor often will be required to work with an estate attorney to prepare the appropriate court pleadings which get signed by the appropriate judge. Then, and only then, will financial institutions, such as banks, credit unions, and brokerage firms, release information and funds to the executor to be held in an estate account while the estate is being settled.

For prospective law firm clients who want to schedule a free 15 minute initial phone call with Paul Rabalais, go to: https://go.oncehub.com/Paul8

This post is for informational purposes only and does not provide legal advice. Please do not act or refrain from acting based on anything you read on this site. Using this site or communicating with Rabalais Estate Planning, LLC, through this site does not form an attorney/client relationship.

Paul Rabalais
Estate Planning Attorney

metadata.title: Text Every Heir on a Probate Lead at Once
metadata.author: Phone Sniper — Real Estate Investor Software
metadata.shortDescription:
Phone Sniper's Heir Research can now find the living relatives behind a probate lead, put their phone numbers on that lead, and text all of them in one campaign, with wording that never uses a name.

Why probate leads go quiet
The name on a probate record is usually the person who died. Text or mail that name and you either reach no one, or you reach a grieving relative with a message addressed to someone who has passed.

The people who can actually make a decision about the house are the heirs and the personal representative. Finding them has meant obituaries, people-search sites, and a spreadsheet for every lead. Most investors skip it, which is why these leads are worth working.

How it works
1. Open a case from the lead. On any contact, click Heir research. The case starts with the owner, the property, and the probate case number already filled in.
2. Find heirs. One click checks the county record on the lead for a personal representative or anyone else on title, and checks your own contacts for the same last name at the same address. Where a skip-trace lookup is enabled on the account, it also looks the property up and returns relatives with phone numbers.
3. Paste an obituary. Copy the "survived by" paragraph from any obituary and paste it in. Phone Sniper reads out the spouse, children, and siblings and adds them as suggestions. One-click links open the free obituary, grave, and people-search sites with the owner already filled in.
4. Confirm the right people. Every name comes in as a suggestion. You confirm the ones that are right and remove the rest.
5. Their numbers land on the lead. Each confirmed heir's phone number is added to the original lead's contact, labelled with who it belongs to, for example "Heir: Rosa Whitman". You get one contact per property instead of five scattered ones.
One campaign texts every heir
Send a campaign to the lead, and every heir number on it gets the text. You don't have to switch on "text every phone number"; heir numbers are treated as separate people automatically.
The wording changes too. Probate leads never get a name in the message, because the name on file is the wrong one. They get a short, soft opener built around the property address:
Hi, this is Brian. Are you still in charge of the house at 412 N Pine St?
Hi, it's Brian. Are you the right person to ask about 412 N Pine St? If taxes are behind, I can cover them and maybe help you keep it.
Every text is worded differently, stays inside one message, and about two-thirds carry a short offer to pay off back taxes or help the family keep the property.

Longer copy for direct mail
Letters and postcards to probate leads use the same idea with more room. The piece is addressed to "Current Resident", names only the property address, and lays out three options:
• Pay off any back taxes owed on the property.
• Work out a way for the family to keep the house, if that's the goal.
• Or buy it as-is, with no repairs, clean-out or commissions, on a timeline that works around the estate paperwork.
It closes by asking the reader to pass the letter along if someone else handles the property. The wording is varied on every piece.
Good to know
• Opt-outs stay personal. If one heir replies STOP, only that heir's number is blocked. The other heirs on the lead can still be reached.
• Flags are visible. A number flagged Do Not Call shows that flag on its label, and your Compliance settings still decide what a campaign is allowed to text.
• Suggestions are leads, not proof. Public records and people-search results can be old or wrong. Who actually inherits depends on the will and state law, so have a title company or probate attorney confirm before closing.
• Everything is logged. The case keeps a research log and a checklist: last deed, death confirmed, probate court searched, every heir identified, taxes and liens checked.

Try it
Open any probate lead in Phone Sniper, click Heir research, then Find heirs. Not on Phone Sniper yet? Start at https://phonesniper.app.

metadata.title: Post-Election Prospecting, Probate Calling Tips & New Holiday Mailers! | ATL Mastermind 602
metadata.author: All The Leads
metadata.shortDescription:
Tune in to our weekly LIVE Mastermind Q+A Podcast for expert advice, peer collaboration, and actionable insights on success in the Probate, Divorce, Late Mortgage/Pre-Foreclosure, Reverse Mortgage, and Aged Expired niches! 

In Episode 602 of the All The Leads Mastermind Podcast, our coaches discuss how the flood of political advertising, phone calls, and direct mail may have affected prospecting results in recent months. As that competition begins to fade, we explore opportunities for agents to reconnect with potential clients, improve call response rates, and make their marketing stand out. We also dive into smarter lead follow-up strategies, including how to organize your pipeline, identify potential spam-labeling issues with your phone number, and adjust your outreach based on different lead types and circumstances. From probate and divorce leads to pre-foreclosure and reverse mortgage prospects, our coaches emphasize the importance of understanding each person's situation and offering solutions rather than pushing for an immediate sale. Plus, hear practical coaching advice on approaching probate families with empathy, building trust through genuine conversations, and developing valuable referral relationships with probate attorneys. We also introduce ATL's new Thanksgiving-themed postcard designs, including larger 6x11 options, created to help agents deliver timely, compassionate messages during a season when families may be discussing important real estate decisions. Whether you're looking to strengthen your prospecting approach, improve your follow-up process, or refresh your direct mail campaigns for the holidays, Episode 602 offers actionable strategies to help you connect with more prospects and make the most of the season. 

 

00:00 Welcome and Introductions 
00:32 How Election Season Impacted Direct Mail Marketing 
03:22 Avoiding Spam-Labeled Calls & Using Local Numbers 
08:49 Smarter CRM Follow-Up & Aging Lead Strategies 
15:48 Lead with Solutions, Not Sales Pitches 
23:41 Approaching Probate Calls with Empathy 
29:36 How to Approach Surviving Spouse Leads 
31:09 Building Trust Through Empathy & Tone 
32:35 Staying Top of Mind with Consistent Follow-Up 
34:57 Why the Holidays Create New Prospecting Opportunities 
36:53 Offering Honest Options to Sellers & Investors 
40:28 Skip Tracing & Probate Attorney Referrals  
50:55 Holiday Card Presentation Begins 

 

Key takeaways 

- Post-election outreach may offer a fresh opportunity. Coaches discussed how political calls, mailers, and ads had crowded communication channels and potentially reduced response rates. 

- Caller ID reputation matters. Agents should periodically check whether their phone number is being flagged as spam, since this can interfere with otherwise legitimate outreach. 

- Different leads require different follow-up timelines. Probate, divorce, and late mortgage prospects face different circumstances, making a strategic CRM-based follow-up process important. 

- Empathy and tone are essential in probate prospecting. Rather than relying on scripted condolences or aggressive sales pitches, agents can focus on listening, understanding the family's situation, and offering helpful resources. 

- Probate attorneys can become valuable referral partners. Attorneys serving as personal representatives may need assistance coordinating practical estate-related tasks, creating opportunities to establish professional relationships. 

- Holiday direct mail can help agents stand out. ATL introduced Thanksgiving-themed postcards with niche-specific messaging and a new 6x11 format intended to attract more attention in the mailbox. 

 

🚀 Subscribe to get notified of our weekly Mastermind calls — every Thursday at 1PM EST! 

👍 Like, Comment, and Share if you found this episode helpful! To learn more, visit  

https://www.AllTheLeads.com or call (844) 532-3369 to check how many leads are available in your market.

metadata.title: The Probate Letter That Actually Gets Callbacks
metadata.author: Probate Mastery
metadata.shortDescription:
Most probate mail gets ignored.

Not because probate leads aren’t interested…

But because the message doesn’t connect.

If you’re sending letters or marketing to probate leads, your touch package matters more than you think.

A strong probate touch package isn’t just about information—it’s about how you communicate during a sensitive situation.

Here’s what makes the difference:

• clear and simple messaging (not overwhelming)
• professional but empathetic tone
• offering help—not just asking for business
• easy ways for them to contact you
• consistency in follow-up touches

Many agents send one letter and expect results.

But successful agents understand that probate leads require:

• patience
• multiple touchpoints
• trust-building over time

Because behind every probate lead is a family navigating a difficult process.

When your message feels helpful instead of sales-focused, you increase your chances of getting a response.

Follow for more insights on:

• probate real estate
• lead generation strategies
• direct mail and marketing
• building a consistent pipeline

metadata.title: Independent Administration of Estates Act (IAEA) in Probate
metadata.author: Meinzer Legal Briefs
metadata.shortDescription:
To learn more about probates, click here:  https://www.meinzerlawoffice.com/probate/

Hi, my name is Andrew Meinzer of Meinzer Law Firm.

Today I am going to talk with you about how to make probates simpler through the Independent Administration of Estates Act.

A California probate decedent’s estate court proceeding (or simply “probate”) is required to transfer the assets of a decedent if the assets at issue exceed a certain value amount.

The California probate is restrictive, cumbersome, and lengthy.  The Independent Administration of Estates Act (or IAEA) is designed to streamline the process, at least a little.

The IAEA removes the requirement that you as the executor or administrator in charge of the probate must obtain court approval prior to taking certain actions.

There are two levels of IAEA authority—full authority and limited authority.

Full IAEA authority provides you the executor or administrator with authority to do anything without prior court approval, except that you do need to obtain prior court approval of the following.  One, paying yourself executor or administrator fees from the probate estate assets.  Paying fees to your attorney from the probate estate assets.  An account petition pertaining to your acts as executor or administrator of the probate.  Distributing probate estate assets to beneficiaries and you being discharged as executor or administrator (although there are some limitations and exceptions to that one).  Plus, generally there are six types of other acts of self dealing involving probate estate assets paying, trading assets with, or otherwise benefiting you as the executor or administrator or your attorney. 

Now limited IAEA authority provides you as the executor or administrator with a few additional limitations.  In addition to those actions that require prior court approval with full IAEA authority, with limited IAEA authority you need to obtain prior court approval of: selling probate estate real property; exchanging probate estate real property; granting an option to purchase probate estate real property; and borrowing money with the loan secured by probate estate real property.

For all actions other than those specific actions that I just mentioned, normally you simply mail a Notice of Proposed Action to all parties interested in the proposed action instead of obtaining prior court approval.

And you must state in that Notice of Proposed Action a specific date on or after which you will take the proposed action.  And that date must be at least 15 days after you mail the Notice of Proposed Action.

And you must file the Notice of Proposed Action with the court.  That way the court knows what’s going on.

Then if none of those parties objects to the action that you described in the Notice of Proposed Action within the required time period, they cannot object to it later.  That enables you as the executor or administrator to take that proposed action safely and without prior court approval.

Finally, whether you have full or limited IAEA authority, there are many actions that you can take without prior court approval and without even mailing and filing a Notice of Proposed Action.

Now, IAEA authority is not automatic.  You must specifically request full or limited IAEA authority to obtain it.

Normally, you do this through the Petition for Probate that you filed with the court.  The Petition for Probate is the first pleading filed with the court that initiated the probate court case.  And through it you also requested that the court appoint you as executor or administrator.

Now, a decedent can prevent you from obtaining IAEA authority, but the only way that they can do that is if they have a will, and the will expressly prohibits IAEA authority.

At Meinzer Law Firm, we have over 20 years of experience helping clients achieve their goals in probate cases.

Again, my name is Andrew Meinzer of Meinzer Law Firm.  If you know that you need our help, or if you just have a question, please contact us and let us take care of you.

A California probate decedent's estate court proceeding, or simply probate, is required to transfer the assets of a decedent if the assets at issue exceed a certain value amount. The California probate is restrictive, cumbersome, and lengthy. The Independent Administration of Estates Act, or IAEA, is designed to streamline the process, at least a little. The IAEA removes the requirement that you, as the executor or administrator in charge of the probate, must obtain court approval prior to taking certain actions. There are two levels of IAEA authority, full authority and limited authority. Full IAEA authority provides you, the executor or administrator, with authority to do anything without prior court approval, except that you do need to obtain prior court approval of the following. One, paying yourself executor or administrator fees from the probate estate assets. Paying fees to your attorney from the probate estate assets. An account petition pertaining to your acts as executor or administrator of the probate. Distributing probate estate assets to beneficiaries and you being discharged as executor or administrator, although there are some limitations and exceptions to that one. Plus, generally there are six types of other acts of self dealing involving probate estate assets paying, trading assets with, or otherwise benefiting you as the executor or administrator or your attorney. Now limited IAEA authority provides you as the executor or administrator with a few additional limitations. In addition to those actions that require prior court approval with full IAEA authority, with limited IAEA authority you need to obtain prior court approval of selling probate estate real property; exchanging probate estate real property; granting an option to purchase probate estate real property; and borrowing money with a loan secured by probate estate real property. For all actions other than those specific actions that I just mentioned, normally you simply mail a Notice of Proposed Action to all parties interested in the proposed action instead of obtaining prior court approval. And you must state in that Notice of Proposed Action the specific date on or after which you will take the proposed action. And that date must be at least 15 days after you mail the Notice of Proposed Action. And you must file the Notice of Proposed Action with the court, that way the court knows what's going on. Then, if none of those parties objects to the action that you described in the Notice of Proposed Action within the required time period, they cannot object to it later. That enables you as the executor or administrator to take that proposed action safely and without prior court approval. Finally, whether you have full or limited IAEA authority, there are many actions that you can take without prior court approval and without even mailing and filing a Notice of Proposed Action. Now, IAEA authority is not automatic. You must specifically request full or limited IAEA authority to obtain it. Normally, you do this through the Petition for Probate that you filed with the court. The Petition for Probate is the first pleading filed with the court that initiated the probate court case. And through it you also requested that the court appoint you as executor or administrator. I'm going to show you everything you need to know. In this video, I'm going to walk you through exactly how to start probate in California. The forms you'll need, where to get them, what they cost, and how to avoid the mistakes that delay families for months. By the end, you'll know exactly how to get probate started and the simple step most families forget to take that adds months of delay to their case. I'll show you how to get this right the first time. Stick with me. Don't skip away to watch cat videos because by the six minute mark, that's where I'll reveal the most common mistake that I see families make when starting probate and how to make sure you don't make the same mistakes and get stuck waiting for continuances and extra hearings. This one thing is so simple, but skipping it can stop your case in its tracks. I'm Gary DeGraziad Jr. Now, I'm not an attorney and I do not offer any legal advice. But for 20 years, I've specialized in probate real estate, helping families navigate the court system and sell the estate home. I don't just help families directly; I also train other real estate agents nationwide how to properly and efficiently handle probate real estate sales. So today, you're not just getting theory or some chat GPT explanation on starting probate. You're getting the exact practical steps that families that I've worked with have used time and time again. I'll show you all the steps you need to follow. First things first, not every estate requires a full probate. California has small estate shortcuts. If the estate is worth less than $208,850 of personal property, you may be able to use a small estate affidavit instead of going through the complete probate process. Starting in April, if the primary residence is valued at $750,000 or less, you may qualify for a simplified transfer process. Why this matters? If you qualify, you can avoid months of paperwork and thousands of dollars in cost. But if there's real estate above those limits, you'll likely need a formal probate. And that's where we start with the petition. Preparation is everything. Before you even file, here are documents that you're going to want to gather: A certified death certificate. The original will. A list of assets like the estate home, any accounts, any vehicles, any business interests. Contact info for all heirs and beneficiaries. Why is this important? Because missing just one relative's address or forgetting to attach the original will can delay your hearing by months. You'll also want to decide who will serve as the personal representative. That's the person who acts on behalf of the estate. When you file, you'll want to request something called IAEA authority. With IAEA full authority, you can manage and even sell real property with far fewer court hearings. Without it, you'll be back in court for approval every time you need to act. Next, you'll file your petition for probate. That's judicial council form DE111, and you can download it right from your county superior courthouse. Now, along with that, you'll file the DE147, the dutiesand liabilities of the personal representative. That's your acknowledgement of what the court expects you to do. When you file, you'll also submit the original will, if there is one, and you'll pay the filing fee, usually a few hundred dollars, depending on the county that you're in. Now, here's where families get tripped up. In the petition, there's a section where you must list all heirs and relatives, even if they're disinherited from the will. You forget one, and the judge will continue your hearing to a later date. And this is that simple mistake I promised earlier for you to avoid. Not listing every required relative in your petition and notice is a huge mistake. It sounds small, I know, but the court is very strict. If an heir is left out, even if they're not inheriting anything, your petition will get delayed. This is one of the most common yet most avoidable mistakes that I see made. After filing, you'll get a hearing date. Then you must notify everyone. Here's how you do that: Complete form DE121, called the Notice of Petition to Administer Estate. Mail it to all required relatives and heirs, but, and this is important, you can't mail it yourself. A non-party must do it, and you must file proof. Publish that notice three times in a qualified newspaper of general circulation wherever the deceased lived. Why this matters? Notice is jurisdictional. If it's not done correctly, the court can't proceed. On your hearing date, if everything is in order, the judge will sign your order for probate, and the clerk will issue your letters of either testamentary or letters of administration. These letters are your proof of authority. With them, you can open estate accounts, pay bills, and most importantly, sell the estate property if needed. Without these letters, you legally cannot act for the estate. Within the first 120 days of getting your letters, you'll have some critical tasks: Open an estate bank account and get an EIN number from the IRS. File your inventory and appraisal (that's the DE160 and 161). A probate referee will value assets. Their fee is 0.1% of the total asset values or a minimum of $75. Send notice to creditors (the DE157) to anyone that the deceased owed money to. Now, these steps matter because they protect the estate. They create a record of assets and liabilities, which the court relies on when approving the distribution letter. So let's quickly review the typical costs to start probate in California: Filing fees, usually a few hundred to several hundred dollars depending on your county. Newspaper publication costs, which are a few hundred dollars more. The probate referee fee, 0.1% of non-cash assets. Bond premiums if a bond is required. Later, attorney fees if you hired counsel and their fee is set by the court. The earlier you file these, the sooner the timeline begins and the sooner you'll have legal authority to act. Starting probate sooner protects the estate's value. Until you have certified letters, you can't manage the property. You can't pay taxes or secure assets. Vacant homes, unpaid bills, family disputes, they only get worse with time. Filing early means you'll have authority within weeks instead of months. So there you go. Episode Summary: 
In this episode of Probate Made Clear, host Michelle Rotella is joined by Renee Spieckermann, founder and principal attorney at RLS Law Corporation. Renee, a California state bar certified specialist in estate planning, trust, and probate law, delves into the complexities of the probate process. 

She explains the stages an estate must complete before probate can close, highlighting factors that influence the timeline, such as court scheduling, creditor claims, and tax matters. Renee also shares insights on how executors can prevent avoidable delays, emphasizing the importance of early document collection and collaboration with probate-savvy real estate agents. Listeners will gain a comprehensive understanding of the probate timeline, enabling them to set realistic expectations and manage the process more effectively.

Key Timestamps:
00:01 – Introduction
00:46 – Initial Stages of Probate
01:19 – Court Timeline Variations
02:14 – Importance of Letters of Administration
03:09 – Creditor Period and Timeline Expectations
04:11 – Average Probate Duration
06:21 – When the Probate Timeline Begins
07:40 – Impact of Court Scheduling
09:48 – Delays from Creditor Claims and Taxes
10:27 – Role of Executor in Managing Delays
13:06 – Selling Real Estate and Probate Delays
14:38 – Steps Executors Can Take to Avoid Delays

About the Show: 
Probate Made Clear is a podcast designed for families, executors, administrators, and beneficiaries navigating the probate process. Hosted by Renee Spieckermann, a seasoned attorney specializing in estate planning, trust, and probate law, the show breaks down complex legal concepts into clear, actionable advice. Each episode offers valuable insights into the probate timeline, legal requirements, and strategies to efficiently manage estates. Whether you're dealing with a simple estate or facing intricate legal challenges, Probate Made Clear provides the guidance needed to make informed decisions and streamline the probate process.

Visit More: https://www.rlsestatelaw.com

#ProbateMadeClear #EstatePlanning #ProbateLaw #ReneeSpieckermann

metadata.author: Win-Win Realtors TV
metadata.shortDescription:
How to make an Overbid on a Probate Property here in California? - This video will give you a general "Overview" on making overbids on Probate properties which require court confirmation.  Court Confirmation is the process by which the probate court has to approve the Sale at a court hearing.  At the Court hearing additional buyers who are allowed to bid on the subject property, including the original buyer. The court conducts the  overbidding process.  The first minimum bid is determined by probate code,  (a formula) and the subsequent bid increases are set by the probate judge.  

There is a probate process via the IAEA (Independent  Administration of Estates Act) in which one does not need approval from the court in order to settle the estate.  The court is still involved however there are fewer changes to  go through and fewer  hoops and restrictions the representatives of the estate.  To start the process the personal representative files a will and all necessary probate forms with the court.  Once all the necessary paperwork has been approved by the court.

metadata.shortDescription:
What is the probate sale overbid process in California? Brendan Mohr, a Greater Sacramento REALTOR and C.A.R. Certified Probate & Trust Specialist, explains how overbidding works at a probate court confirmation hearing and what buyers, executors and administrators should understand before the hearing.

When a California probate real estate sale requires court confirmation, accepting an offer does not necessarily mean that buyer will ultimately purchase the property.

At the court confirmation hearing, another qualified buyer may have an opportunity to submit a higher bid.

California probate law establishes a formula for determining the initial minimum overbid. Once a qualifying overbid is made, additional bidding may take place at the hearing until the court determines the successful buyer.

This can create a very different real estate transaction from a traditional home sale.

The original buyer needs to understand that the property may still be purchased by someone else at the confirmation hearing. Potential overbidders need to understand the court's requirements and be prepared to complete the purchase if their bid is accepted.

For the executor or administrator, proper marketing before the hearing can also be important. Additional buyer interest and competitive bidding can potentially increase the amount ultimately received by the estate.

Court confirmation and overbidding are most commonly associated with probate real estate sales involving Limited Authority. Understanding the process before accepting an offer can help the personal representative, buyers and real estate agents avoid surprises later.

metadata.shortDescription:
What is a probate real estate auction in California? Brendan Mohr, a Greater Sacramento REALTOR and C.A.R. Certified Probate & Trust Specialist, explains what people often mean by a probate auction and how the California probate court overbid process works.

Not every probate house in California is sold at an auction.

The term "probate auction" is often used to describe what happens when a probate real estate sale requires court confirmation.

Typically, the personal representative first lists and markets the property, accepts an offer and then petitions the probate court to confirm the sale.

At the court confirmation hearing, other qualified buyers may have an opportunity to submit a higher bid. This is commonly called the probate overbid process.

If a qualifying overbid is made, additional bidding can occur at the hearing, and the court ultimately confirms the sale to the successful buyer.

This process is very different from a foreclosure auction. The property has generally already been marketed by a Realtor and an initial buyer has already entered into a purchase agreement before the court hearing.

Probate sales handled with Full Authority under California's Independent Administration of Estates Act can generally be completed without this court confirmation and overbid process after applicable probate requirements are satisfied.

metadata.title: LA Probate Overbids: 1 in 6 Court Confirmation Sales Get Overbid
metadata.author: Bill Gross, the LA Probate Expert
metadata.shortDescription:
How often does a Los Angeles County probate court confirmation sale get overbid? I've attended close to a thousand court sales and tracked the data for the last seven years. Of the 275 sales I could verify in the MLS, 43 were overbid at the confirmation hearing. That's about 1 in 6, which means money was left on the table 1 in 6 times. Every attorney, fiduciary, and listing agent should be ready for an overbid, even if you don't expect one.

In this video for probate attorneys, fiduciaries, and listing agents, I cover:
1. 1 in 6 court confirmation sales gets overbid (43 of 275 verified sales)
2. The median overbid was $47,500, or 6.7% over the accepted offer. The minimum overbid is 5% plus $500.
3. Properties over $1 million are more likely to be overbid, and those overbidders are usually retail buyers buying for themselves
4. Keep marketing until the hearing: clear instructions in the agent remarks, make reports available, allow inspections, and share every photo you have
5. An overbidder must bring a cashier's check for 10% of the overbid price, made out to the estate (no personal checks), with no contingencies, and it's generally non-refundable if they win
6. Overbids don't have to slow the close. In my data, overbid sales actually closed a little sooner than sales with no overbid.
7. Three practical steps for attorneys and fiduciaries: keep the original buyer engaged as a backup, vet the overbidders, and submit the order at the hearing and get a certified copy to escrow fast

Limited authority (IAEA): court confirmation IS required. Full authority: court confirmation MAY BE required (for example, if a beneficiary objects to the sale).

Ask the Expert: Probate | Ep. 6 — The Overbid Process Explained: How Probate Court Protects Heirs From a Low Sale Price

Most people have no idea that when a probate property sale requires court confirmation, the courtroom itself can turn into an auction.

In Episode 6 of Ask the Expert: Probate, I walk through one of the most unique and misunderstood aspects of probate real estate — the overbid process. This is the mechanism the California probate court uses to ensure that heirs and beneficiaries receive the absolute highest possible price for an estate property — and it works in a way that most buyers, sellers, and even real estate agents have never encountered before.

In this episode we cover:

What court confirmation means for a probate sale
Not every probate sale requires court confirmation — but when it does, the rules change significantly. We break down what triggers court confirmation and what it means for everyone involved in the transaction.

How the overbid process works
Once a property is accepted by the court for confirmation, outside buyers have the opportunity to appear in court and bid against the original accepted offer in an auction-style process. Frank explains exactly how that process unfolds from start to finish.

Why the overbid process ultimately protects the heirs
Far from being an obstacle, the court confirmation and overbid process exists specifically to protect the estate and ensure heirs receive the maximum value from the sale of their inherited property.

Whether you are an heir, an administrator, or a buyer interested in purchasing a probate property — this episode gives you a clear picture of one of the most distinctive processes in all of California real estate.

metadata.title: Can You Avoid Court Confirmation in Probate if an Heir Objects in California? | Brendan Mohr
metadata.author: Sell a House in Probate California | Brendan Mohr
metadata.shortDescription:
Can you avoid court confirmation when an heir objects to the sale of a California probate house? Brendan Mohr, a Greater Sacramento REALTOR and C.A.R. Certified Probate & Trust Specialist, explains how an heir's objection can affect a probate real estate sale under the Independent Administration of Estates Act (IAEA).

With Full Authority, an executor or administrator can often sell California probate real estate without a court confirmation hearing after following the required Notice of Proposed Action process.

But what happens when an heir or other interested person objects?

A timely objection can prevent the personal representative from simply proceeding with the proposed sale under the normal Notice of Proposed Action procedure. That doesn't necessarily mean the heir has an absolute veto over selling the property or that every objection automatically results in a court-confirmed sale.

The next step can depend on the circumstances. The objection might be resolved or withdrawn, the terms of the sale could change, or court involvement may become necessary to determine whether the transaction can proceed.

This is why an objection should be taken seriously, particularly when the estate has already accepted an offer or the property has ongoing expenses.

Executors and administrators should understand how their authority, the Notice of Proposed Action and an heir's objection can affect the timing and structure of the sale.

metadata.shortDescription:
What is a probate sale without court confirmation in California? Brendan Mohr, a Greater Sacramento REALTOR and C.A.R. Certified Probate & Trust Specialist, explains how a Full Authority probate real estate sale can often proceed without a court confirmation hearing.

Not every California probate house sale has to go back to court before it can close.

When an executor or administrator has Full Authority under the Independent Administration of Estates Act, the personal representative can generally sell estate real property without a court confirmation hearing when the required probate procedures are followed.

This can make the real estate transaction look much more like a traditional California home sale.

The property can be prepared for market, listed on the MLS, shown to buyers and placed under contract. The personal representative can negotiate the price and terms of the sale without asking the probate judge to select the buyer at a confirmation hearing.

However, Full Authority doesn't mean there are no probate requirements.

The Notice of Proposed Action process can be an important part of a Full Authority sale. Interested persons who are entitled to notice generally receive information about the proposed transaction and have an opportunity to object.

If the required procedures are completed and there is no timely objection requiring a different course, the sale can generally proceed without court confirmation.

That is very different from a Limited Authority probate sale, where the sale of real estate generally requires court confirmation and may be subject to probate overbidding.

Understanding whether the personal representative has Full or Limited Authority is therefore one of the first things a probate Realtor should determine before listing the property.

metadata.title: Probate Overbid Auction: Watch a Real Los Angeles Sale
metadata.author: Bill Gross, the LA Probate Expert
metadata.shortDescription:
This is a real probate court confirmation auction in Los Angeles, the kind where buyers can overbid the accepted offer. Watch how it plays out.
Buying at a probate overbid? Here's what your Realtor does and what your attorney does: https://www.thelaprobateexpert.com/blog/probate-overbid-buyer-realtor-or-attorney

This property being auctioned is at 7534 W. 81ST STREET, PLAYA DEL REY, CA 90293 (technically in the city of Los Angeles).

When most people think of auctions, they think of sales at the county steps, usually done for all cash, and an opportunity for significant savings.

A probate court confirmation auction is where the court has a sale but ALSO allows overbidding (under specific conditions) to make sure the best price is obtained by the estate. In California, these terms require a bidder to show up with a cashier's check for 10% of the opening bid and be willing to buy the property "as is" with no contingencies, be able to close in as little as 11 days, often without any prior access to the property.

This auction is what I would term a "retail auction" where the property happens to be a probate sale. These generally occur when several heirs cannot agree on a list price or a sale price, so they use the auction to attempt to get the best price. 

Perspective buyers are lured in by the prospects of buying a property well below market, in this case for the list of $1,200,000 when in actuality it sold at auction for $2,050,000. And, in this case, even that buyer will likely have to hope that no one overbids them at a court confirmation sale auction to be scheduled.

About 60 parties showed up, and it looks like approximately 20-30 were registered to bid on this property.

metadata.title: What is a Probate Sale With Court Confirmation | Brendan Mohr
metadata.author: Sell a House in Probate California | Brendan Mohr
metadata.shortDescription:
What is a probate sale with court confirmation in California? Brendan Mohr, a Greater Sacramento REALTOR and C.A.R. Certified Probate & Trust Specialist, explains how a court-confirmed probate real estate sale works and why it is different from a traditional home sale.

Some California probate properties can be sold without a court confirmation hearing. Others require the accepted sale to be brought before the probate court for approval before the transaction can proceed toward closing.

One of the biggest factors is the authority granted to the executor or administrator.

When a personal representative has Limited Authority under the Independent Administration of Estates Act, the sale of real property generally requires court confirmation.

The process can include obtaining the required appraisal, marketing the property, accepting an offer and petitioning the probate court to confirm the sale.

The confirmation hearing is particularly important because the accepted buyer may not necessarily be the final buyer. Other qualified purchasers can potentially appear at the hearing and submit a higher bid under California's probate overbid procedures.

That makes a court-confirmed probate sale different for sellers, buyers and real estate agents.

The executor or administrator needs to understand the additional procedures and timing involved. Buyers need to understand that an accepted offer may still be subject to court approval and possible overbidding. The Realtor needs to understand how the real estate transaction fits into the probate court process.

Topics include:
